Case: Sangeeta Devi W/O Sh. Vinod Kumar Singh vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
Court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Pilot Court), Karkardooma Courts, Delhi (2018)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: claim_petition
Issues: rash_negligent_driving, negligence_proof, compensation_quantum, loss_of_dependency, multiplier, section_166, just_compensation
Vehicles: motorcycle
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Deceased child Shivam (aged approximately 10 years, born 2005) died on 14.01.2014 after being hit by motorcycle No. DL 3SBY5198 near Annpurna Mandir, Sonia Vihar, Delhi The motorcycle was driven rashly and negligently at high speed by respondent Mahesh Chand Shivam was taken to Jag Pravesh Chandra Hospital and then Lok Nayak Hospital where he died on the same day Claimant is the mother of the deceased child Respondent did not file a reply or lead evidence despite opportunities No insurance company was made a party; liability fastened solely on respondent-driver
Holdings: Compensation for death of a child is computed using the notional income formula laid down by Delhi High Court in MAC Apps. No. 554/2010, with inflation correction using Cost Inflation Index from the base year 1997-98 and age-appropriate multiplier. For a child aged up to 10 years the multiplier of 10 is applied and an equal amount is added as composite non-pecuniary damages. Uncontested FIR and criminal record, coupled with absence of any defence evidence, is sufficient to prove rash and negligent driving on a preponderance of probability standard.
Outcome: DAR petition allowed. Respondent directed to pay compensation of Rs. 5,74,000/- with interest at 9% p.a. from date of filing till realisation.
The claimant-mother Sangeeta Devi filed a DAR petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, claiming compensation for the death of her 10-year-old son Shivam, who was killed on 14.01.2014 near Annpurna Mandir, Sonia Vihar, Delhi. The deceased was hit by motorcycle No. DL 3SBY5198 driven rashly and negligently by respondent Mahesh Chand. The respondent neither filed a reply nor led evidence, and the criminal record along with the mother's testimony established negligence on a preponderance of probability. On the quantum, the Tribunal applied the formula prescribed by the Delhi High Court for deaths of children: the notional income of Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule) was inflation-corrected using the Cost Inflation Index for 2013-14 (CII 939 against base 331), yielding a notional income of Rs. 43,000 p.a. After one-third deduction for personal expenses and applying a multiplier of 10 (appropriate for age group up to 10 years), the pecuniary loss to estate was Rs. 2,86,667. An equal amount was added as composite non-pecuniary damages, yielding total compensation of Rs. 5,74,000. Interest was awarded at 9% p.a. from the date of filing. The award was made solely against the respondent-driver.

Case: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
Court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (2005)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: contributory_negligence, compensation_quantum, multiplier, income_determination, future_prospects, insurance_liability, interest_on_compensation, section_166
Vehicles: jeep, scooter
Stance: claimant_supporting, insurer_supporting, mixed
Facts: Dr. Kamlesh Kumar, an Eye Surgeon aged 43 years, was killed on 12 August 1996 when a jeep bearing No. P.42-A 0174 hit his scooter No. U.P. 42/1395 from behind near Ayodhya The jeep was owned by Madan Mohan Sonkar and insured with New India Assurance Company Ltd.; the driver Gaya Prasad held a valid driving licence MACT-II Additional District Judge, Faizabad awarded Rs. 16,09,000 with 9% p.a. interest by judgment dated 7 August 2001 The insurer filed F.A.F.O. No. 510/2001 challenging the award amount; the claimants filed F.A.F.O. No. 509/2001 seeking enhancement Monthly salary of deceased at the time of death was Rs. 9,776 (old scale) revised to Rs. 12,593 (5th Pay Commission scale) from 01.01.1996 Tribunal applied multiplier of 10 instead of the correct multiplier of 12 for age 43
Holdings: When the jeep hit the deceased's scooter from behind, findings of rash and negligent driving negate any case of contributory negligence; no separate finding on contributory negligence is necessary where the facts are self-speaking. An insurer who has no valid defence under Section 149(2) has no right to challenge quantum of compensation without permission under Section 170 of the MV Act. Where the Tribunal's formula under Susamma Thomas leads to the same figure as would result from the correct multiplier applied to revised salary, there is no ground for interference. Interest on compensation may be reduced to 7.5% per annum having regard to prevailing bank rates.
Outcome: Both appeals disposed of with a modification: the rate of interest was reduced from 9% to 7.5% per annum. The award amount of Rs. 16,09,000 was confirmed. The share of minors was directed to be deposited in a nationalised bank in fixed deposits till majority.
Two First Appeals arose from the same MACT award of Rs. 16,09,000 with 9% interest, passed by MACT-II Additional District Judge, Faizabad, for the death of Dr. Kamlesh Kumar (Eye Surgeon, aged 43) who was knocked down by a jeep from behind while riding his scooter in Ayodhya on 12 August 1996. The insurer (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) appealed challenging the quantum, while the claimants (widow, minor children and father) appealed for enhancement. The High Court rejected the insurer's contributory-negligence argument because the undisputed finding was that the jeep struck the scooter from behind, making any question of the deceased's negligence self-evidently untenable. The insurer's challenge to the multiplier (10 instead of 12) was also rejected on the ground that the overall compensation figure was correct when the Tribunal's formula was read as a whole — and in any case the insurer had no standing to challenge quantum without Section 170 permission. The claimants' enhancement appeal was dismissed because the compensated amount would not materially change even if the revised pay scale and future prospects were considered. The sole modification was a reduction of the interest rate from 9% to 7.5% p.a. to align with prevailing bank rates.

Case: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Mr. Subbaray and Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd.
Court: III Additional Judge and Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Court of Small Causes, Bengaluru (SCCH-18) (2024)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: claim_petition
Issues: driving_license_validity, license_breach_defence, insurance_liability, pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, compensation_quantum, rash_negligent_driving, section_166
Vehicles: car
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: On 09.01.2021 at about 5.30 p.m., petitioner Sunil Shreesail Killiket was a passenger in car No. KA-03-AC-5300 near MG Patel Hospital, Indi, Vijayapura when the driver Appu drove it rashly and negligently, causing the car to fall and rotate on the roadside Petitioner sustained spinal cord injury (C7-T1), underwent surgery (laminectomy and C4-D2 fusion), and was left in wheelchair with 90% whole body disability and 100% functional disability Medical expenses incurred of Rs. 14,85,260/-; petitioner was 25 years old at the time of accident Insurer's defence: driver had no valid driving licence; vehicle used without valid permit and fitness certificate Tribunal found the driver did not possess a driving licence; breach of fundamental condition proved by insurer Insurer nonetheless directed to pay compensation to the third-party petitioner under the 'pay and recover' principle
Holdings: A third party petitioner cannot be made to suffer due to the fault of the owner in allowing an unlicensed driver; the insurer must pay the compensation first and recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' doctrine. Where functional disability is 100%, future prospects at 40% must be added to notional income for computing loss of future earnings; multiplier of 18 applies for age 25. Attendant charges are awarded using the multiplier method (Rs. 8,000/month x 12 x 18) for permanently disabled victims who require lifetime care. Loss of marriage prospects is a compensable head for a victim with 90% whole body disability.
Outcome: Petition allowed in part. Total compensation of Rs. 87,49,500/- awarded against Respondent No. 1 (owner). Insurer directed to pay first under 'pay and recover' principle with liberty to recover from Respondent No. 1. Interest at 6% p.a. on Rs. 68,21,500/- from date of petition till realisation.
Petitioner Sunil Shreesail Killiket (25 years) sustained catastrophic spinal cord injuries on 09.01.2021 when a car driven by an unlicensed driver overturned near Vijayapura, leaving him in a wheelchair with 90% whole body and 100% functional disability. He filed a claim under Section 166 of the MV Act against the vehicle owner and Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd. The Tribunal found rash and negligent driving proved. The insurer established that the driver had no valid driving licence, which constituted a fundamental breach of policy, and was held not liable to indemnify the owner. However, applying the 'pay and recover' principle (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba; Shamanna v. Oriental Insurance), the insurer was directed to pay the compensation first with liberty to recover from the owner. Compensation totalling Rs. 87,49,500/- was awarded, including Rs. 45,36,000 for future loss of income (notional income Rs. 15,000/month + 40% future prospects x multiplier 18 x 100% disability), Rs. 14,85,260 medical expenses, Rs. 17,28,000 attendant charges, Rs. 3,00,000 loss of marriage prospects, and other heads. Interest awarded at 6% p.a. on the principal sum (excluding attendant charges and future medical expenses).

text:
Case: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
Court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru (Special Full Bench) (2020)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, policy_breach, pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, commercial_vehicle_use, permit_violation, section_166, license_breach_defence
Vehicles: tempo, goods_carriage, commercial_vehicle
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: Claimant Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharanakeri was travelling as a coolie/gratuitous passenger in Tempo No. KA-28/B-5434 (a goods vehicle) from Tikota to Dhulkhed village for coolie work on 24.04.2006 The tempo's driver drove rashly near Horti village on NH-13, the vehicle turned turtle and the claimant sustained grievous injuries MACT-V, Bijapur awarded compensation of Rs. 1,000/- with 6% p.a. interest and directed New India Assurance Co. to pay and recover from owner (Respondent No. 2) The insurer appealed arguing it was not liable since the claimant was a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle — a policy breach under Section 149(2) Learned Single Judge referred two questions to a Full Bench: (I) whether a contractual policy with extra premium makes insurer liable to pay and recover for any breach; (II) whether 'pay and recover' rule applies in view of Section 149 mandate
Holdings: Tribunals and High Courts — and not only the Supreme Court under Article 142 — have the power to pass a 'pay and recover' order against an insurer that has proved a defence under Section 149(2) of the MV Act. A 'fundamental breach' of a policy condition is one which is referable to the cause of the accident; but even a fundamental breach does not automatically absolve the insurer of its liability to pay the third party — it only entitles the insurer to recover from the insured. The insurer can be completely absolved of liability only where the third party/victim was individually or in collusion with the insured responsible for the breach of a fundamental condition. The 'main purpose rule' requires that conditions in an insurance policy be interpreted so that no innocent third party suffers for a breach of condition for which they had no responsibility. A pay and recover order is an exercise of discretion based on facts and circumstances of each case; the court must give appropriate reasons.
Outcome: Appeal dismissed. Full Bench held that Tribunals and High Courts can pass 'pay and recover' orders even when the insurer has proved a breach of policy under Section 149(2), subject to the exception of fraud or collusion by the victim with the insured. The only circumstance where the insurer can be completely absolved is if the third party/victim was responsible for or complicit in the breach.
In this Special Full Bench judgment of the Karnataka High Court (three judges), the court answered a reference arising from MFA No. 30131/2010 in which the New India Assurance Co. challenged a Tribunal order directing it to pay Rs. 1,000 compensation and recover from the insured for injuries to a coolie (Yallavva) travelling as a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (Tempo KA-28/B-5434) that overturned on 24.04.2006. The insurer argued the breach (gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle) was a fundamental breach under Section 149(2) and that only the Supreme Court under Article 142 could order 'pay and recover.' After exhaustively analysing Sections 146, 147 and 149 of the MV Act, the Full Bench held: (1) Tribunals and High Courts can pass 'pay and recover' orders; this power is not exclusive to the Supreme Court. (2) A 'fundamental breach' is one causally connected to the accident, but even proving such a breach does not completely absolve the insurer vis-à-vis an innocent third party. (3) The 'main purpose rule' — protecting innocent third parties — means the insurer's inter-se dispute with the insured cannot affect the third party's right to compensation. (4) Complete absolution is possible only if the victim/third party was responsible for or in collusion with the insured in causing the breach. The appeal was dismissed.

text:
Case: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Ellappa and others
Court: High Court of Judicature at Madras (2009)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, commercial_vehicle_use, permit_violation, compensation_quantum, section_166
Vehicles: tempo, goods_carriage, commercial_vehicle
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: On 21.06.1991, a large group of persons was travelling in tempo TN-29 Y-1724 towards Thenkanikottai on Kelamangalam-Parandur road; at about 9.00 a.m. the driver drove rashly and the vehicle capsized near Koottur diversion road, injuring many and killing some The owner-cum-driver Kuttiappan was carrying paying passengers (52 persons) in the goods vehicle, which is not authorised under the policy National Insurance Co. Ltd. had insured the vehicle and contested liability on two grounds: (i) goods vehicle not authorised to carry passengers, (ii) driver had no valid driving licence at the time MACT, Hosur held the insurer liable and fixed quantum of compensation in various amounts across 11 petitions Full Bench of Madras HC in Nagammal's case (2009-I-CTC-1) had already settled that insurer is not statutorily required to cover liability for passengers in a goods vehicle Madras HC applied its own Full Bench guidelines (Nagammal) but exercised discretion to pass 'pay and recover' order due to the claimants being poor village residents who had been litigating since 1996
Holdings: Passengers travelling in a goods vehicle — whether gratuitous or paying — are not covered under the insurance policy and the insurer has no statutory liability to pay them compensation. Notwithstanding the absence of statutory liability, the court can exercise discretion to direct 'pay and recover' in appropriate cases, particularly where the claimants are poor and have been litigating for years. The insurer, once directed to pay and recover, can initiate execution proceedings against the insured directly without filing a fresh suit.
Outcome: All 11 civil miscellaneous appeals disposed of. Common award of the Tribunal as to quantum confirmed. Insurer directed to pay compensation to claimants first and to recover the same from the owner-cum-driver (Kuttiappan/first respondent in MCOPs) by filing execution proceedings directly before the concerned court.
Eleven Civil Miscellaneous Appeals were filed by National Insurance Co. Ltd. challenging MACT awards arising from the capsizing of goods tempo TN-29 Y-1724 on 21.06.1991 near Koottur, in which a large group of persons travelling as passengers sustained injuries and some died. The insurer contested liability on the basis that the passengers were travelling in a goods vehicle without authorisation and that the driver had no valid licence. Following the Full Bench ruling in Nagammal's case (2009-I-CTC-1), the Madras High Court reiterated that persons travelling as passengers in goods vehicles — whether gratuitous or paying — are not covered under the insurance policy and the insurer has no statutory obligation to compensate them. The owner-cum-driver Kuttiappan was held personally liable. However, exercising discretion given the poverty of the claimants and the fact they had been litigating since 1996, the court directed the insurer to pay the compensation first and recover it from the insured by executing the award directly before the executing court without needing to file a fresh suit. The quantum awarded by the Tribunal was confirmed without modification.

Case: The Manager, New India Assurance Co. Ltd. vs Chennamma and others
Court: High Court of Judicature at Madras (2013)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: driving_license_validity, license_breach_defence, insurance_liability, pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, compensation_quantum, loss_of_dependency, section_166
Vehicles: lorry, truck, goods_carriage, commercial_vehicle, motorcycle
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: On 5.10.2002 at 1.45 p.m., deceased Venkata Kondaiya (aged 38 years, Rivetter Grade II at Chennai Port Trust, earning Rs. 10,395/month) was riding his Hero Honda motorcycle TN-22 Y 1596 on Chennai-Minjur Road near Pungambedu bus stand when lorry TN-20 Z 3024 (belonging to 5th Respondent M/s Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd.) driven rashly in the opposite direction dashed against the motorcycle; deceased succumbed at Stanley Government Hospital Claimants (widow, minor children, mother) filed claim petition claiming Rs. 30,00,000/-; MACT, Tiruvallur awarded Rs. 12,89,500/- with pay and recover order against insurer Insurer's defence: driver held only LMV (light motor vehicle) licence; the lorry was a 'heavy goods vehicle' (GVW 16,200 kg); driver lacked valid licence to drive HGV Registration Certificate (Ex.P8) confirmed lorry as 'Heavy Goods Vehicle' with GVW 16,200 kg exceeding the 12,000 kg threshold in Section 2(16) Driver's history sheet (Ex.R1) showed licence for 'light motor vehicle' with an endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle' but no separate endorsement for 'heavy goods vehicle' Owner remained ex parte before the Tribunal
Holdings: For a goods vehicle the gross vehicle weight (not unladen weight) determines vehicle classification; a lorry with GVW of 16,200 kg is a 'heavy goods vehicle' under Section 2(16) of the MV Act. An endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle' on an LMV licence does not authorise driving a 'heavy goods vehicle'; a separate endorsement is required for HGV. When the driver of a vehicle did not have a valid driving licence to drive that category of vehicle, this constitutes a breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii); however, as a third-party claim this does not exonerate the insurer — a 'pay and recover' order is appropriate. In third-party risks cases the insurer has to indemnify the claimant and recover from the insured; the insurer cannot disown liability merely because the driver held a licence for a different category of vehicle.
Outcome: Appeal dismissed. Tribunal's award of Rs. 12,89,500/- confirmed. Insurer directed to pay and recover from 5th Respondent (owner M/s Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd.) as per the mode stated in Nanjappan's case. 4th Claimant (Ramulamma) having died, her share to be apportioned equally among remaining claimants.
The widow, minor children and mother of Venkata Kondaiya (Rivetter at Chennai Port Trust, aged 38) challenged a MACT award which directed the insurer (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) to pay Rs. 12,89,500/- and recover from the lorry owner (M/s Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd.) after the lorry TN-20 Z 3024 fatally knocked down the deceased's motorcycle on 5.10.2002. The insurer appealed arguing the driver had only an LMV licence with a 'transport vehicle' endorsement and lacked a specific HGV licence, so it should be fully absolved. The Madras High Court undertook a detailed analysis of Sections 2(16), 2(21) and 2(47) of the MV Act and the Central Government's vehicle-classification notifications. It held that the lorry with a gross vehicle weight of 16,200 kg was unambiguously a 'heavy goods vehicle', and that a 'transport vehicle' endorsement on an LMV licence does not extend to driving an HGV. The breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) was thus proved. However, following the consistent Supreme Court position (Swaran Singh, Iyyappan, Laxmi Narain Dhut), the court held that in third-party risk cases the insurer must indemnify first and recover from the insured. The quantum (Rs. 12,89,500/-) and interest (7.5% p.a.) were confirmed unchanged. The appeal was dismissed.

text:
Case: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
Court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad (2019)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, policy_breach, pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, commercial_vehicle_use
Vehicles: jeep
Stance: insurer_supporting, adverse_to_claimant
Facts: On 15.04.2012, deceased Suryakant Pandurang Nikam (aged 50) was travelling as a passenger in Tata Sumo jeep No. MH 23/E-3762 on Tandulja-Ambajogai road after attending a marriage ceremony at village Padoli, when driver-cum-owner Abdul Gazi lost control near Amba Sakhar Karkhana petrol pump at about 4.00 p.m.; the vehicle got skid, hit a bridge railing and overturned Suryakant succumbed to injuries after 17 days of hospitalisation (Ashwini Accident Hospital, YCM College Hospital and Civil Hospital, Latur) Claimants (widow and two sons) claimed Rs. 7,50,000/-; MACT, Latur awarded Rs. 7,79,800/- with interest against the insurer jointly and severally with owner-driver, with a pay and recover order Insurance company's defence: the vehicle was a private jeep, but respondent No. 4 (owner) was carrying the deceased for hire or reward (jeep hired by Sheshrao for his son's marriage); this was a wilful fundamental breach of the Act policy (Section 149(2)(a)(ia)) No additional premium was paid for passenger risk; the policy was an Act policy Tribunal found the breach proved but still directed pay and recover; High Court reversed this
Holdings: A passenger in a private vehicle plied for hire or reward against the Act policy is not a 'third party' within the meaning of Section 147 of the MV Act; the risk of such occupant is not covered under an Act policy. Where the risk of the deceased passenger is not covered under the Act policy and the deceased cannot be termed a 'third party', the Tribunal cannot pass a 'pay and recover' order against the insurer. The insurer must be completely exonerated, not merely subjected to pay and recover, when the deceased's claim falls entirely outside the statutory coverage.
Outcome: Appeal partly allowed. MACT award set aside to the extent of holding the insurance company liable jointly and severally. Claim as against the insurance company dismissed. Claimants directed to recover compensation solely from opponent No. 1 (driver-cum-owner Abdul Gazi). Insurance company's deposited amount to be returned.
United India Insurance Co. Ltd. challenged a MACT award (Latur) directing it to pay Rs. 7,79,800/- compensation jointly and severally with the driver-cum-owner for the death of Suryakant Pandurang Nikam, who was travelling in a private Tata Sumo jeep (MH 23/E-3762) being operated for hire for a marriage ceremony. The insurer proved that the deceased was travelling for hire or reward in a private vehicle — a wilful fundamental breach of the Act policy under Section 149(2)(a)(ia) — and that no additional premium had been paid for passenger coverage. The Bombay High Court (Aurangabad Bench) followed New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Asha Rani (AIR 2003 SC 607) and subsequent Supreme Court decisions to hold that occupants of private vehicles plied for hire or reward are not 'third parties' under Section 147 of the MV Act and are not covered by the Act policy. Since the deceased was not a third party, the court held that no 'pay and recover' order could be passed against the insurer, distinguishing cases like Shamanna (which involved an unlicensed driver carrying a genuine third party). The insurer was completely exonerated and the claimants were directed to recover compensation solely from the driver-cum-owner.

text:
Case: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
Court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad (2014)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, insurance_liability, policy_breach, commercial_vehicle_use, section_166, maintainability
Vehicles: tempo, tractor, goods_carriage, commercial_vehicle
Stance: insurer_supporting, adverse_to_claimant
Facts: Five consolidated first appeals by United India Insurance Co. Ltd. challenging Claims Tribunal awards directing pay-and-recover FA 3852/2008: deceased Chandrakantbhai was travelling as gratuitous passenger in a Matador Tempo bearing No.GJ.5T-2312 carrying his goods; driver drove rashly causing death FA 710-713/2007: tractor No.GAO-6007 accident causing death of Parvatiben Tejabhai and injuries to other claimants who were travelling on the mudguard/tractor In all cases, insurance policies were 'Act only' policies not covering gratuitous passengers Claims Tribunals had held insurance companies not liable but directed them to pay compensation and recover from owner (pay-and-recover direction) Insurance companies challenged the pay-and-recover direction as beyond statutory power
Holdings: Gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles are not 'third parties' covered under Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and an 'Act only' policy does not cover such risk. Section 149(4) and (5) operate only in respect of liabilities required to be statutorily covered or covered by the policy; they cannot be invoked for gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles. Neither the Claims Tribunal nor the High Court in section 173 appellate jurisdiction has power to issue pay-and-recover directions where the risk is neither statutory nor covered by the policy. Supreme Court pay-and-recover directions in earlier cases involving gratuitous passengers (Baljit Kaur, Saju Paul) were exercises of power under Article 142 of the Constitution, not precedents under section 149.
Outcome: All five appeals allowed. Insurance companies exonerated. Impugned awards modified so that only the driver and owner of the vehicle are liable to pay compensation; insurance companies stand exonerated from such liability.
In five consolidated first appeals before the Gujarat High Court, the central issue was whether, where a Claims Tribunal found an insurance company not liable to indemnify the insured under an 'Act only' policy (because victims were gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles), the Tribunal or High Court could still direct the insurer to first pay compensation and then recover from the owner. The cases involved a Matador tempo accident (FA 3852/2008) and a tractor accident (FA 710-713/2007). The court held that gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles are not 'third parties' under Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Section 149(4) and (5) operates only for third-party risks and risks required to be statutorily covered. The Claims Tribunal and High Court, exercising powers under sections 166 and 173, have no authority to issue pay-and-recover directions for non-statutory, non-third-party risks. Any such direction by the Supreme Court in prior cases (Baljit Kaur, Challa Bharathamma, Saju Paul) was under Article 142 of the Constitution, not under section 149. Affirming the co-ordinate bench decision in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lilaben, the court allowed all appeals, exonerated the insurance companies, and restricted liability to the vehicle owners and drivers.

Case: Dadapeera S/O Abdul Salam Sab vs Mallesh M S/O Hanumanthappa
Court: High Court of Karnataka, Dharwad Bench (2025)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, third_party_liability, pay_and_recover, policy_breach, compensation_enhancement, compensation_quantum, income_determination, just_compensation
Vehicles: tractor, trailer
Stance: insurer_supporting, adverse_to_claimant
Facts: Accident on 28.07.2011 during agricultural tilling operations at Kamalapura village Claimant Dadapeera (20-year-old agricultural coolie) was sitting on mud-guard of tractor engine (tractor and trailer KA-35/T-9766) during field tilling Driver Mallesh M drove the tractor rashly and negligently causing the tractor to turtle; claimant fell and sustained fracture of left femur and left leg Claims Tribunal (MVC No.300/2013) awarded Rs.84,160/- with interest; held driver and owner liable; exonerated National Insurance Co. Ltd. Claimant appealed for enhancement of compensation; insurer's exoneration was not challenged by claimant Full Bench of Karnataka High Court in Gadhilingappa's case had already held person sitting on mud-guard of tractor is not covered under s.147(1) MV Act
Holdings: A person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor is not required to be covered by statutory insurance under section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as held by the Full Bench of the Karnataka High Court in Gadhilingappa's case. The defence available to the Insurance Company is violation of Rule 28 of Rules of Road Regulations, 1989 (person sitting on mud-guard), which is not a defence under section 149(2) of the MV Act; therefore pay-and-recover order cannot be made. Compensation under the heads of loss of income, pain and suffering, loss of amenities, medical expenses, and incidental charges was enhanced; notional income taken as Rs.6,000/- per month and functional disability at 8% (from 20% physical disability) with multiplier of 18.
Outcome: Appeal partly allowed. Compensation enhanced from Rs.84,160/- to Rs.2,33,680/- with interest at 6% per annum from date of petition till realisation. Insurance company's exoneration upheld. Only owner (Hussain Sab Bavaji) and driver (Mallesh M) are liable to pay the enhanced compensation.
A claimant-appellant aged 20 sustained fracture injuries to his left femur and left leg on 28 July 2011 while sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor engine during field tilling at Kamalapura village. The driver lost control, causing the tractor to turtle. The Claims Tribunal (MVC No.300/2013) awarded Rs.84,160/- but exonerated the insurer (National Insurance Co. Ltd.), holding only owner and driver liable. The Karnataka High Court upheld the insurance company's exoneration on the basis of a Full Bench ruling (Gadhilingappa's case) that persons sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor are not covered under section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The court further held that while the claimant's presence on the mud-guard violated Rule 28 of the Rules of Road Regulations, 1989, this did not constitute a section 149(2) defence and therefore pay-and-recover order could not be made. On quantum, the court enhanced compensation significantly to Rs.2,33,680/-, taking notional income of Rs.6,000/- per month, functional disability of 8% from 20% physical disability, and multiplier of 18, plus adding amounts for pain and suffering, loss of amenities, incidental expenses, and medical expenses. The appeal was partly allowed: insurer exonerated, only owner and driver liable for the enhanced compensation.

text:
Case: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
Court: Supreme Court of India (2007)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: fake_license, driving_license_validity, license_breach_defence, insurance_liability, third_party_liability, pay_and_recover, policy_breach
Stance: insurer_supporting, adverse_to_claimant
Facts: Civil Appeal No. 1140 of 2007 and connected appeals by National Insurance Co. Ltd. challenging High Court and Consumer Forum decisions Multiple High Courts and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission had applied the Swaran Singh ratio to own-damage claims (first-party insurance disputes) — not third-party claims In several cases, insurer's defence of fake driving licence was not accepted on the basis that Swaran Singh's liberal approach applies to all motor accident cases Some cases involved fake licences that had subsequently been renewed, with forums holding the renewal cured the defect Appellants argued that Swaran Singh applies only to third-party risk cases under section 149, not to own-damage or consumer disputes
Holdings: The decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh has no application to cases other than third-party risks under section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Where originally the licence was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality; a fake licence cannot be transformed into a genuine one by any subsequent renewal. In cases of third-party risks the insurer must indemnify the amount and may, if so advised, recover the same from the insured. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to section 149 of the Act; the statute is beneficial only qua the third party, not the owner of the offending vehicle.
Outcome: All appeals allowed. High Courts and Consumer Commissions directed to reconsider matters afresh in light of the principles laid down: Swaran Singh applies only to third-party risk; fake licence renewal cannot cure the defect; purposive interpretation does not apply to section 149 cases.
Multiple civil appeals before the Supreme Court addressed a common question: whether the principles of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, relating to third-party claims under section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, apply to own-damage claims and Consumer Forum matters. High Courts and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission had extended Swaran Singh beyond third-party cases, holding insurers liable in own-damage contexts even where the driver had a fake licence or where the licence had been forged and subsequently renewed. The Supreme Court held categorically that Swaran Singh was rendered in the context of section 149, which governs only third-party risk, and has no application to own-damage cases or Consumer Forum disputes. The Court further held that a fake driving licence cannot be cured by any subsequent renewal, as no licensing authority has power to renew a fake licence and transform it into a genuine one. The distinction arises because section 149 creates a statutory fiction between third parties and insurers, while own-damage cases are pure contractual matters between insured and insurer where no such fiction operates. For third-party risks, the insurer must indemnify and may recover from the insured. Purposive interpretation applicable to third-party cases does not apply to own-damage cases under section 149. The High Courts and Commissions were directed to reconsider matters afresh in accordance with these principles.

text:
Case: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
Court: Supreme Court of India (2013)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: driving_license_validity, license_breach_defence, insurance_liability, third_party_liability, commercial_vehicle_use, section_166
Vehicles: taxi, commercial_vehicle
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: On 23.05.1998 at about 8.30 PM, deceased Charles was riding his bicycle when driver Sivananayaitha Perumal drove a Mahindra van at high speed and dashed against Charles, causing his death Driver held a valid LMV (light motor vehicle) driving licence but had no specific endorsement for driving the Mahindra van as a commercial vehicle (taxi) The vehicle was being used as a taxi (commercial vehicle) at the time of accident Claims Tribunal awarded Rs.2,42,400/- with interest; the insurer challenged the award before the High Court High Court exonerated the insurer, holding that the driver was not duly licensed to drive a commercial vehicle as he lacked an endorsement for driving commercial vehicles Owner S. Iyyapan appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court judgment
Holdings: A Mahindra Maxi Cab is a light motor vehicle; a driver holding a valid LMV licence is entitled to drive it without needing a separate endorsement for use as a commercial vehicle. An insurer cannot disown its third-party liability on the ground that although the driver held a valid LMV licence, there was no endorsement to drive the LMV when used as a commercial vehicle. The statutory right of a third party to recover compensation from the insurer cannot be defeated merely by absence of a commercial vehicle endorsement when the vehicle qualifies as a light motor vehicle. Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 mandates compulsory third-party insurance to ensure that victims of accidents can get compensation; this purpose is defeated if insurers can avoid liability on technical licensing grounds.
Outcome: Appeal allowed. Impugned judgment of the High Court set aside. Insurer held liable to pay the compensation so awarded to the dependants of the victim of the fatal accident.
The Supreme Court considered whether an insurance company could avoid its statutory third-party liability to pay compensation to a motor accident victim on the ground that the driver of the offending vehicle held a valid light motor vehicle (LMV) licence but had no specific endorsement for driving the vehicle when used as a commercial vehicle (taxi/Mahindra Maxi Cab). The deceased, Charles, was killed on 23 May 1998 when the driver of a Mahindra van drove at high speed and hit his bicycle. The Claims Tribunal awarded Rs.2,42,400/- with interest. The High Court exonerated the insurer, holding that a driver using a vehicle as a commercial taxi without a commercial vehicle endorsement was not duly licensed. The Supreme Court reversed this, holding that the Mahindra Maxi Cab was a light motor vehicle and a driver holding a valid LMV licence was duly authorised to drive it. No separate commercial vehicle endorsement was required when the vehicle qualifies as an LMV. The Court reiterated that Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act mandates compulsory third-party insurance specifically to ensure victims receive compensation, and the insurer could not disown its statutory liability on technical licensing grounds. The insurer was held fully liable to pay the award; recovery from the insured remains available in the event of an actual policy breach.

Case: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
Court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi (2013)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, pay_and_recover, third_party_liability, driving_license_validity, license_breach_defence, commercial_vehicle_use, compensation_quantum, compensation_enhancement, loss_of_dependency, future_prospects
Vehicles: tempo, goods_carriage, commercial_vehicle
Stance: claimant_supporting, insurer_supporting, mixed
Facts: Accident on night of 11-12 September 2005 on Outer Ring Road, Delhi; Tempo No. UP-12K-5797 was travelling loaded with guava (fruit) when driver Sunil Kumar drove at high speed, causing the vehicle to overturn after a tyre burst Five claim petitions: deaths of Naresh Kumar @ Setu (aged 18, son of Harpal Singh) and Naresh Kumar son of Kashmira (aged 21), plus injuries to three others Insurance company proved that driver Sunil Kumar held only a Light Motor Vehicle (Non-Transport) licence and was driving a goods vehicle (commercial vehicle) — breach of policy conditions established Insurance company did not challenge liability in three injury cases; challenged only in death cases (MAC APPs 138/2011, 143/2011, 744/2011) Claims Tribunal had granted recovery rights to insurer and held insurer liable to pay despite proven breach; claimants appealed for enhancement of quantum Key factual dispute: whether deceased were gratuitous passengers or owners/representatives of goods being transported
Holdings: Evidence established that the two deceased were travelling as owners/representatives of goods (guava) and not as gratuitous passengers; the insurance company could not avoid its liability to them as third parties. The insurance company's statutory liability to satisfy a third-party award is not defeated by a proven breach of policy conditions; it must pay the compensation and can recover from the insured/tortfeasor. No addition towards future prospects is permissible for self-employed or temporarily employed workers (following Reshma Kumari three-Judge Bench). The owner and driver who did not appeal the recovery rights granted by the Tribunal remain bound by that finding.
Outcome: MAC APPs 30/2012 and 138/2011 (Harpal Singh): compensation enhanced to Rs.4,38,000/-. MAC APPs 744/2011 and 143/2011 (Satto): compensation enhanced to Rs.3,75,000/-. Insurance company held liable to pay with recovery rights against owner (Mohd. Qayum) and driver (Sunil Kumar). No addition for future prospects as deceased were self-employed/temporary workers.
Four connected appeals arose from a tempo accident on the night of 11-12 September 2005 in Delhi when the driver lost control after a tyre burst, killing two passengers and injuring three others. The insurance company (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) proved that the driver held only a Light Motor Vehicle (Non-Transport) licence but was driving a commercial goods vehicle — an established breach of policy conditions. The central issues were: (1) whether the two deceased were gratuitous passengers or owners of goods, and (2) whether the insurer remained liable despite proven breach. The Delhi High Court held that evidence proved both deceased were travelling as owners/representatives of goods (guava) and were not mere gratuitous passengers, so the insurer could not avoid liability on that ground. As regards the licence breach, the court confirmed that the insurance company's statutory obligation to pay third-party compensation survives a proven policy breach; the insurer pays and recovers from the owner/driver. On quantum, following Reshma Kumari (three-Judge Bench), no addition towards future prospects was permitted for self-employed or temporary workers. Compensation for Harpal Singh's son was enhanced to Rs.4,38,000/- and for Satto's son to Rs.3,75,000/-, with recovery rights preserved for the insurer against the owner and driver.

text:
Case: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
Court: High Court of Karnataka (2001)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: driving_license_validity, license_breach_defence, insurance_liability, third_party_liability, pay_and_recover, compensation_quantum, compensation_enhancement, negligence_proof
Vehicles: lorry, motorcycle
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: Case 1 (MVC 177/1997, M.F.A. 5566/1999 by insurer and 690/2000 by claimant): Minor girl Suma (3 years old, right leg amputated above knee, 80% permanent disability) was hit by lorry MYT 6600 on 13.01.1997 while standing by the roadside; driver's licence had expired on 28.11.1996 and was renewed only on 17.01.1997 — 50-day gap; insurer appealed against Tribunal's joint liability finding Case 2 (MVC 140/1994, M.F.A. 3557/1998 by owner): Inthu Pasha (20 years, pillion rider on motorcycle) died on 19.01.1994 when hit by Canter lorry KA 18-240 owned by K.G. Srinivasamurthy; driver's licence had expired 05.07.1993 and was renewed 24.02.1994 — 7-month 20-day gap; Tribunal dismissed claim against insurer; owner K.G. Srinivasamurthy appealed In both cases, insurer's defence was that drivers had no valid (effective) driving licence on the date of accident due to licence expiry Insurance policy condition in both cases used the word 'and' (not 'or') connecting 'not duly licensed' and 'disqualified' Both drivers had been licensed since the early 1980s and had renewed consistently, except for the gaps on the accident dates
Holdings: The insurance company's liability to satisfy an award against a third party is a statutory liability not inhibited by policy conditions; breach of policy conditions cannot bind the third party. Mere expiry of a driving licence and failure to renew it as on the date of accident — without the driver being disqualified — does not amount to breach of the exclusion clause where the exclusion clause uses 'and' to connect 'not duly licensed' and 'disqualified'. Where the breach alleged is not a factor that contributed to causing the accident, it is not a fundamental breach; the exclusion clause must be read down to serve the main purpose of the policy, i.e., to indemnify the insured. In both cases, the insurance company failed to prove willful breach of policy conditions and therefore cannot recover the amount paid from the insured.
Outcome: M.F.A. No. 5566/1999 (insurer's appeal in MVC 177/1997) dismissed; insurer remains jointly liable with owner. M.F.A. No. 690/2000 (claimant's appeal) partly allowed; compensation enhanced to Rs.3,50,000/- with interest at 9% p.a. Cross-objection No. 23/2000 allowed in part (interest rate aspect). M.F.A. No. 3557/1998 (owner's appeal in MVC 140/1994) allowed; insurer held jointly and severally liable with owner; compensation enhanced to Rs.1,95,000/- with interest at 9% p.a. No recovery order made since insurer failed to prove breach.
A Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court consolidated four appeals arising from two separate motor accident cases. In MVC No. 177 of 1997, a minor girl Suma had her right leg amputated above the knee after being hit while standing by the roadside; in MVC No. 140 of 1994, Inthu Pasha (20 years) died as a pillion rider on a motorcycle. In both cases, insurers argued that the drivers lacked valid driving licences on the accident date as licences had expired and were renewed only thereafter (50-day gap in the first case; 7-month gap in the second). The court held comprehensively: (1) the insurance company's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory and is not defeated by policy conditions; (2) mere expiry of a driving licence without disqualification does not constitute a breach of the exclusion clause, particularly where the clause uses 'and' (requiring both unlicensed and disqualified) rather than 'or'; (3) where the breach does not contribute to causing the accident, it is not a fundamental breach and the exclusion clause must be read down; and (4) the insurers in both cases failed to prove willful breach, so no recovery could be ordered. The insurer's appeal in the first case was dismissed; the owner's appeal in the second case was allowed with insurer held jointly liable. Compensation was enhanced to Rs.3,50,000/- and Rs.1,95,000/- respectively with interest at 9% per annum.

Vehicles: taxi, commercial_vehicle
Stance: mixed, insurer_supporting
Facts: Accident on 07.07.2002: claimant V. Vijayakumar (22 years, B.Com graduate, working as accountant at Rs.4,500/month) was walking on road near Annur Bus Stand when Tourist Maxi Cab (Mahendra van TN 27 L 3638) driven by 3rd respondent Marimuthu dashed into him Claimant sustained severe head injuries — diffuse axonal injury and corpus callosum involvement; admitted to KMCH ICU for 5.5 months; on ventilator 46 days; tracheostomy performed At time of trial, claimant was totally paralysed, non-communicative, in vegetative existence; permanent disability assessed at 95% Driver (3rd respondent) had only LMV licence (No.1407/97) valid up to 05.06.2016 but had no authorisation (badge) to drive a transport vehicle (Tourist Maxi Cab) R.W.1 (Junior Assistant from Motor Vehicles Inspector's office) testified that 3rd respondent was not granted any authorisation to drive transport vehicle nor allotted a badge number Claims Tribunal awarded Rs.19,59,895/- including Rs.8,20,800/- for permanent disability and Rs.9,37,095/- for medical expenses; held insurer jointly and severally liable Insurer appealed challenging both liability and the quantum as excessive
Holdings: The insurance company discharged its burden of proving that the 3rd respondent (driver) had only an LMV licence and lacked the specific authorisation (badge) required to drive a transport vehicle (Tourist Maxi Cab), establishing a breach of policy conditions under section 149(2)(a)(ii). Absence of badge/authorisation for transport vehicle proved by R.W.1's evidence that no badge was allotted and by the absence of endorsement in the driving licence; the Tribunal erred in fastening statutory liability on the insurer. Despite the insurer proving breach of policy conditions, a pay-and-recover order is the appropriate remedy: the insurer must pay compensation to the innocent claimant and can then recover from the insured/owner. Total compensation of Rs.19,59,895/- including Rs.8,20,800/- for permanent disability (Rs.4,500 x 12 x 16 x 95/100) and Rs.9,37,095/- for medical expenses with interest at 9% per annum is just, reasonable, and not excessive given the 95% disability and vegetative existence.
Outcome: Appeal partly allowed. Quantum of Rs.19,59,895/- with 9% interest per annum confirmed as just and reasonable. Award modified: insurance company is not jointly and severally liable but must pay the compensation to the claimant (1st respondent) and then recover the same from the insured (owner C. Marimuthu and driver). Insurer entitled to file execution petition against respondents 3 and 4 in the same proceedings.
A Madras High Court Division Bench heard an appeal by United India Insurance Company Limited challenging both liability and quantum in an award of Rs.19,59,895/- for a severe road accident. On 7 July 2002, V. Vijayakumar (22 years, B.Com graduate, accountant earning Rs.4,500/month) sustained severe head injuries when the driver of a Tourist Maxi Cab (Mahendra van) drove rashly and hit him while walking near Annur Bus Stand. The driver was convicted. The claimant suffered diffuse axonal injury, became totally paralysed, entered vegetative existence (95% permanent disability), and spent 5.5 months in ICU on ventilator. The insurer proved that the driver held only an LMV licence without the specific transport vehicle badge/authorisation required under Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicles Rules. The court accepted this defence: the driver was not duly licensed for the transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab), establishing violation of policy conditions under section 149(2)(a)(ii). However, applying the Kamla/Swaran Singh doctrine, the court modified the award so that the insurer must pay compensation to the claimant and then recover from the owner/insured. The quantum of Rs.19,59,895/- (including Rs.8,20,800/- for permanent disability and Rs.9,37,095/- for medical expenses) with 9% interest was maintained as just and reasonable given the severity of injuries.

Case: Tarachand Raosaheb Chaudhari vs The Oriental Insurance Co Ltd
Court: Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Mumbai, Bench at Aurangabad (2024)
Legal area: consumer; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, policy_breach, evidence_appreciation, other
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: Multiple appellants availed the Corona Rakshak Policy from Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. and paid premiums. Each appellant was diagnosed COVID-19 positive by RTPCR during the policy period and admitted to a Covid care centre declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation for more than 72 hours on medical advice. Oriental Insurance repudiated all claims on the ground that the Covid centres were quarantine centres and not hospitals under clause 3.6 of the policy. District Consumer Commission, Aurangabad dismissed all original consumer complaints. Appellants challenged the dismissal orders before the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in First Appeal Nos. 619 to 623 of 2022.
Holdings: A Covid care centre designated by the government or Municipal Corporation for Covid-19 treatment qualifies as a hospital under clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy. Repudiation of insurance claims solely on the ground that a Municipal Corporation-declared Covid centre is not a hospital constitutes deficiency in service by the insurer. An insured who was corona positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours on medical advice of a qualified practitioner is entitled to the full sum insured under the Corona Rakshak Policy.
Outcome: All five first appeals partly allowed. District Commission orders quashed. Oriental Insurance directed to pay Rs. 2,50,000/- under Corona Rakshak Policy with interest at 8% p.a. from the respective dates of repudiation plus Rs. 10,000/- for mental agony and litigation costs in each case.
This combined judgment of the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (Aurangabad Bench), delivered on 21 October 2024, decides five first appeals (FA Nos. 619-623/2022) challenging dismissals of consumer complaints against Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. for repudiating claims under the Corona Rakshak Policy. Each appellant tested COVID-19 positive during the policy period, was referred by the Aurangabad Municipal Corporation's Medical Officer to a designated Covid care centre (MIT Boys Hostel, Samajkalyan Boys Hostel, or Government Engineering College Covid Centre), and was admitted for more than 72 continuous hours on medical advice. The insurer repudiated all claims arguing the Covid centres were quarantine centres, not hospitals under clause 3.6 of the policy, and that no active line of treatment was given. The District Consumer Commission had dismissed the original complaints. On appeal, the State Commission held that clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy expressly includes any government-designated setup for Covid-19 treatment as a hospital, that the Municipal Corporation-declared Covid centres fell within this definition, and that the insurer's repudiation was deficiency in service. Each appellant, having satisfied the twin conditions of confirmed Covid-positive diagnosis and hospitalization exceeding 72 hours on medical advice, was held entitled to Rs. 2,50,000/- with 8% p.a. interest from the date of repudiation plus Rs. 10,000/- for mental agony and costs.

Case: Bhagyashree Santosh Galande vs The Oriental Insurance Co Ltd
Court: Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Mumbai, Bench at Aurangabad (2024)
Legal area: consumer; stage: appeal
Issues: insurance_liability, policy_breach, evidence_appreciation, other
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: Multiple appellants availed the Corona Rakshak Policy from Oriental Insurance and paid premiums ranging from Rs. 2,580/- to Rs. 5,185/-. Each appellant was diagnosed Covid-positive by RTPCR during the policy period and admitted to a Covid centre declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation for more than 72 hours on medical advice. Oriental Insurance repudiated claims asserting Covid centres were quarantine centres and not hospitals under policy clause 3.6, and that there was no active line of treatment during hospitalization. District Consumer Commission, Aurangabad dismissed the consumer complaints in CC Nos. 334, 335, 374, 375, and 336 of 2021 on 26.07.2022. Appellants filed First Appeal Nos. 619-623 of 2022 before the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
Holdings: A government-designated Covid care centre run under municipal authority with medical practitioners and qualified nursing staff qualifies as a hospital under clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy. Repudiation of a claim when the insured was demonstrably Covid-positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours on medical advice amounts to deficiency in service. The District Commission erred in dismissing the complaints by ignoring evidence that appellants met the eligibility criteria under clause 2 and 4.1 of the Corona Rakshak Policy.
Outcome: All five appeals partly allowed. District Commission orders dated 26.07.2022 quashed. Oriental Insurance directed to pay Rs. 2,50,000/- per claimant under Corona Rakshak Policy with 8% p.a. interest from the respective repudiation dates plus Rs. 10,000/- for mental agony and costs.
This combined judgment of the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (Aurangabad Bench), dated 21 October 2024, contains five appeal judgments (FA Nos. 619-623 of 2022) against the District Consumer Commission's dismissal of complaints under the Corona Rakshak Policy issued by Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. Each appellant was RTPCR-confirmed Covid-positive and admitted to a Municipal Corporation-declared Covid care centre in Aurangabad for hospitalization exceeding 72 hours on medical advice. The insurer repudiated all claims under clause 3.6 of the policy, contending Covid centres were quarantine facilities rather than hospitals with active treatment. The State Commission examined clause 3.6(vi), which includes any government-designated setup for Covid-19 treatment as a hospital, and held that Municipal Corporation-declared Covid centres with qualified medical staff squarely fell within this definition. The insurer's repudiation was found to be deficiency in service. All claims were allowed for Rs. 2,50,000/- each with 8% p.a. interest from the date of repudiation and Rs. 10,000/- towards mental agony and costs. The District Commission's orders were quashed. This judgment confirms that Covid-era pandemic care centres with government designation and qualified staff meet the policy definition of hospital under similar insurance products.

Case: M/S Crown Consultants (P) Ltd. vs The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi (2011)
Legal area: consumer; stage: suit
Issues: insurance_liability, policy_breach, limitation, evidence_appreciation, other
Stance: insurer_supporting, adverse_to_claimant
Facts: Complainant M/s Crown Consultants (P) Ltd., a stockbroker and NSE member, suffered a loss of Rs. 43,05,032/- in share purchase transactions on behalf of client Babu Lal Sethia during 01-03 May 1996 after being allegedly deceived by an unidentified person impersonating Sethia on telephone. The complainant lodged an insurance claim on 30.06.1996 under an NSE-negotiated policy with Oriental Insurance covering member stockbrokers against specified perils including deception as to identity of any person. Oriental Insurance repudiated the claim on three grounds: (i) claim filed more than 30 days after crystallisation of loss on 07.05.1996; (ii) member-constituent agreement not executed on stamp paper as per NSE/SEBI rules; (iii) client codes not entered contemporaneously in trades as per NSE rules. The complainant argued the loss crystallised only on 01.06.1996 after exhaustive enquiries at Barmer, and the NSE regulations cited were not in force in May 1996. The National Commission found the complainant's conduct inconsistent with genuine deception and failed the burden of establishing the insured peril under Section 1(c) of the policy.
Holdings: The burden of proving that a loss was caused by the insured peril rests on the assured; the complainant failed to discharge this burden in respect of the alleged deception. A contract of insurance is governed by the doctrine of utmost good faith (uberrima fides); the complainant's conduct showed lack of even ordinary good faith throughout. The claim was filed well beyond the 30-day period from the date of discovery/awareness of the loss; the insurer committed no deficiency in service in treating the delay as uncondonable. A stockbroker's failure to follow NSE regulatory requirements in executing large trades on behalf of a new client without adequate margin is inconsistent with the due diligence required for a valid insurance claim.
Outcome: Original complaint dismissed as totally devoid of merit or good faith. No deficiency in service found on the part of the insurer in repudiating the insurance claim.
This original complaint (Complaint Case No. 121 of 1999) before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, decided on 31 May 2011, concerns a stock-broking firm's claim for indemnification of Rs. 43,05,032/- under an NSE-negotiated insurance policy covering stockbrokers against various risks including deception as to the identity of persons placing orders. Crown Consultants alleged that an unidentified caller impersonated client Babu Lal Sethia and placed large share purchase orders during 01-03 May 1996, resulting in a loss after prices fell. The insurer repudiated the claim citing delayed filing (30 days from loss), non-execution of member-constituent agreement on stamp paper, and non-entry of client codes at the time of trading. The Commission conducted a thorough factual examination and found the complainant's narrative of deception implausible and internally inconsistent when compared across the first information report, the complaint filed three years later, and affidavits filed after twelve years. The Commission held that the doctrine of utmost good faith pervades an insurance contract from formation through claim, that the complainant breached NSE regulations by trading for Nahata without a separate member-constituent agreement, and that the delay in filing was uncondonable. The complaint was dismissed entirely, with no deficiency in service found on the insurer's part.

Case: Smt. Kamla Devi vs Government Of NCT Of Delhi And Anr.
Court: High Court of Delhi (2004)
Legal area: other; stage: writ
Issues: compensation_quantum, loss_of_dependency, multiplier, other
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Uday Singh, an electrician from Wazirpur, Gurgaon, died on 20.04.1996 in a bomb blast at Arjun Guest House, Paharganj, Delhi, caused by a terrorist who assembled an improvised explosive device (RDX) in the building. Sixteen other persons also died in the blast. The terrorist was a member of a Jammu and Kashmir terrorist organisation and died in the explosion. The Government of NCT of Delhi paid an ex-gratia amount of Rs. 50,000/- to the petitioner Kamla Devi (widow), which she regarded as grossly inadequate. Petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 226 seeking a writ of mandamus directing respondents to pay Rs. 10 lakhs or adequate compensation for the State's failure to protect the life of her husband under Article 21 of the Constitution. At the time of death, Uday Singh was 29 years old, earning Rs. 3,000/- per month, leaving behind wife Kamla Devi and infant son Mukesh (aged 4 months).
Holdings: The State owes a duty to protect the life and liberty of innocent citizens under Article 21 and when it fails to prevent terrorism resulting in death, it is liable to compensate the victim's family under public law jurisdiction. Compensation for crime victims can be awarded by High Courts under Article 226 without relegating them to civil courts; such public law compensation is in addition to private law tort remedies. Compensation comprises two parts: a standard conventional sum for non-pecuniary losses (revised periodically for inflation using CPI-IW) and dependency compensation computed by the multiplier method using the Second Schedule of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 as a guide. The standard conventional sum for non-pecuniary losses for the year 1996 was held to be Rs. 97,700/- (inflation-corrected from Rs. 50,000/- set in Lata Wadhwa for 1989).
Outcome: Writ petition allowed. State directed to pay Rs. 4,36,500/- (after adjusting ex-gratia of Rs. 50,000/-) with simple interest at 7% p.a. from 20.04.1996 (date of explosion) till date within four weeks. The compensation comprised standard conventional sum of Rs. 97,700/- (inflation-adjusted) and dependency compensation of Rs. 3,88,800/- computed using the multiplier method.
This writ petition (decided 10 September 2004 by the Delhi High Court) was filed by Kamla Devi, widow of Uday Singh who died in the Paharganj bomb blast of 20 April 1996 caused by a terrorist. Uday Singh was 29 years old and earned Rs. 3,000/- per month at the time of death. The petitioner sought Rs. 10 lakhs compensation from the State for failing to prevent the terrorist attack in violation of the constitutional guarantee under Article 21. The court held that the State, having failed to prevent terrorism resulting in the death of an innocent citizen, is liable to pay compensation in public law jurisdiction under Article 226. Rejecting the view that petitioners must pursue private law tort remedies, the court adopted a two-tier compensation formula drawing on D.K. Basu, Lata Wadhwa, and the Motor Vehicles Act Second Schedule: a standard conventional sum for non-pecuniary loss (revised to Rs. 97,700/- using CPI-IW inflation adjustment from the 1989 Lata Wadhwa benchmark of Rs. 50,000/-) plus dependency compensation using the multiplier of 18 (applicable to age 29) yielding Rs. 3,88,800/-. After adjusting the ex-gratia of Rs. 50,000/- already paid, the State was directed to pay Rs. 4,36,500/- with 7% simple interest from the date of death. The judgment is an important precedent on the methodology of inflation-adjusted conventional sums and crime-victim compensation under public law.

Case: A.V. Janaki Amma And Ors. vs Union Of India (Uoi) And Ors.
Court: High Court of Andhra Pradesh (2003)
Legal area: other; stage: writ
Issues: evidence_appreciation, vicarious_liability, compensation_quantum, other
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Smt. Savithri, wife of Major P. Gopalakrishna (a Commissioned Officer in the Indian Army), died on 16.02.1997 after surgery at Military Hospital, Secunderabad. A cystectomy surgery was performed on 26.11.1996 by Col. M.N. Nath (Obstetrician and Gynaecologist); a surgical mop was negligently left inside Savithri's abdomen during the operation. Despite persistent post-operative symptoms including fever and wound discharge, Savithri was not referred to a specialist and was prematurely discharged. On 01.01.1997, Savithri was taken to Apollo Hospital where exploratory laparotomy revealed the mop; she ultimately died on 16.02.1997 from septicemia and multi-organ failure. A Court of Inquiry confirmed the negligence and recommended disciplinary action against Col. M.N. Nath and censure against Brig. S.V. Vatve; the findings were accepted by the General Officer Commanding.
Holdings: Principle of res ipsa loquitur applies where a surgical mop is left inside a patient's abdomen; the respondent doctors were grossly negligent. When a fundamental right to life under Article 21 is violated by the negligence of a public authority's employees, the State is vicariously liable and compensation is awardable in public law under Article 226. Public law compensation for violation of Article 21 is a palliative remedy in addition to private law tort remedies; it is based on strict liability and the defence of sovereign immunity is inapplicable. The Court of Inquiry's findings of gross negligence, when produced before the court and accepted by the appropriate superior authority, constitute strong evidence of medical negligence.
Outcome: Writ petition allowed. Union of India directed to pay Rs. 3,00,000/- apportioned as Rs. 50,000/- each to petitioners 1 and 4, and Rs. 1,00,000/- each to petitioners 2 and 3. Medical expenses of Rs. 2,99,241/- at Apollo Hospital were separately reimbursed by the President of India. Petitioners given liberty to file civil suit, with any civil damages to be adjusted against the public law award.
This writ petition (decided 23 October 2003 by the Andhra Pradesh High Court) arises from the death of Smt. Savithri, wife of Major P. Gopalakrishna, due to medical negligence at Military Hospital, Secunderabad. During surgery for an ovarian cyst on 26 November 1996, Col. M.N. Nath (Senior Advisor, Gynaecology) left a surgical mop inside Savithri's abdomen. Despite post-operative complications including persistent fever and wound discharge, she was not referred to a specialist and was prematurely discharged. When admitted to Apollo Hospital in January 1997, the mop was discovered; she died on 16 February 1997 from septicemia and multi-organ failure. A Court of Inquiry assembled in November 1997 confirmed gross negligence, attributing blame to Col. M.N. Nath for leaving the mop, concealing the information, and failing to take corrective measures, and to the Commandant for not investigating adequately. The court applied res ipsa loquitur and held the doctors grossly negligent. On the public law remedy, the court surveyed landmark decisions from Rudul Shah to D.K. Basu, holding that violation of Article 21 through State medical negligence attracts compensatory relief in writ jurisdiction. The Union of India was directed to pay Rs. 3,00,000/- apportioned among petitioners and was permitted to recover from the negligent doctors. Petitioners were also left free to pursue civil remedies, with any civil award to be adjusted.

Case: Mrs. M. Rathnamma and Others vs ICICI Lombard General Ins. Co. Ltd. and Another
Court: IX Additional Small Causes Court and Additional MACT, Bangalore (SCCH-7), M.V.C. No. 2107/2015 (2016)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: claim_petition
Issues: section_166, rash_negligent_driving, insurance_liability, driving_license_validity, permit_violation, compensation_quantum, loss_of_dependency, future_prospects, multiplier, consortium
Vehicles: bus, commercial_vehicle
Stance: claimant_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: On 01.04.2015 at about 10.15 p.m., M. Eshwarappa (aged 32, Security Guard earning Rs. 11,970.55 per month) was walking on the extreme left edge of Bangalore Main Road near Chandu Motors, Singasandra. Bus bearing Registration No. KA-51-C-114, owned by M/s. Megha Travels and insured by ICICI Lombard, driven rashly and negligently at high speed, dashed into the deceased and fled the spot, leaving the bus near Madiwala Traffic Police Station. Deceased was shifted to LIVE 100 Hospital where he was declared dead; post mortem confirmed cause of death as injuries to head and spinal cord. Electronic City Traffic Police registered FIR and filed charge sheet against the driver for offences under IPC s.279, 304A and MV Act s.134(a), (b) and 187. Insurer ICICI Lombard contested the claim raising defences of invalid driving licence, absence of permit and fitness certificate, but did not produce any evidence on its behalf.
Holdings: Eye-witness testimony corroborated by FIR, complaint, charge sheet, spot panchanama, MVI report, inquest and post mortem report conclusively established rash and negligent driving by the bus driver as the cause of death. The insurer failed to produce any evidence to substantiate its specific defences of invalid driving licence or absence of permit/fitness certificate; violation of policy terms by the owner was accordingly not proved. For a deceased aged 32 years in permanent salaried employment, future prospects are computed by adding 50% of actual income per the Rajesh v. Rajbir Singh formula; with 3 dependants, 1/3rd of total income is deducted as personal expenses, and a multiplier of 16 is applied. A father cannot be considered a dependant upon his son for the purposes of motor accident compensation.
Outcome: Petition partly allowed. ICICI Lombard directed to pay Rs. 25,95,346/- with interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition till payment. Insurer's defences (invalid licence, no permit/fitness) rejected as not proved. Father (petitioner No. 3) held not entitled to dependency but recognized as legal representative. Amount to be shared in ratio 50:20:10:20 among petitioners 1-4.
This MACT award (M.V.C. No. 2107/2015, dated 19 October 2016) concerns the death of M. Eshwarappa, a 32-year-old security guard earning Rs. 11,970.55 per month, who was fatally struck by a privately operated mini bus (KA-51-C-114) while walking on the extreme left edge of Bangalore Main Road on 01 April 2015. The bus driver fled the scene after the impact. The owner M/s. Megha Travels remained ex-parte. ICICI Lombard, the insurer, contested the claim raising defences of invalid driving licence and absence of permit and fitness certificate, but produced no evidence. The Tribunal, relying on the eye-witness account of P.W.2, corroborated by FIR, charge sheet, spot sketch, MVI report and post mortem, held rash and negligent driving conclusively proved. All insurer defences were rejected for want of evidence. Following Rajesh v. Rajbir Singh (2013) for future prospects (50% addition for age below 40), Sarla Verma for multiplier (16 for age 32) and deduction (1/3rd for personal expenses with 3 dependants), the Tribunal computed loss of dependency at Rs. 22,98,346/-. Additional heads included consortium (Rs. 1,00,000/-), loss of care and guidance for minor child (Rs. 1,00,000/-), funeral expenses (Rs. 25,000/-), loss of love and affection (Rs. 25,000/-), transportation of body (Rs. 7,000/-) and loss of estate (Rs. 40,000/-). Total compensation: Rs. 25,95,346/- at 9% interest.

text:
Case: Nazar Singh vs State Of Punjab And Others
Court: High Court for the States of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh (2013)
Legal area: service_employment; stage: writ
Issues: insurance_liability, vicarious_liability, other
Stance: owner_driver_supporting, adverse_to_insurer
Facts: Petitioner Nazar Singh, a driver employed by Punjab Roadways, was driving bus PBM-6964 on 12.02.1985 when it met with an accident in village Mander area, resulting in two deaths and two injuries. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), Ludhiana, by award dated 02.06.1986 held the petitioner negligent and the employer Punjab Roadways paid Rs. 3,10,427.95/- in compensation to the accident victims. Punjab Roadways issued a show cause notice in 1992 seeking recovery of Rs. 2,12,000/- with 9% interest from the petitioner-driver, and passed an order dated 24.02.1994 directing recovery of Rs. 3,10,427.95/- without conducting any departmental inquiry. The bus was not insured; the State of Punjab had not established a statutory compensation fund as required by the proviso to Section 146(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 as a precondition for exempting State transport vehicles from mandatory insurance. In the proceedings before the MACT, Punjab Roadways had itself contested the claim supporting the driver's plea that he was not negligent, only for the employer to later seek full recovery from the same driver.
Holdings: The MACT award, standing alone, cannot form the basis of recovery of compensation from the driver-employee; a prior departmental inquiry with effective opportunity of hearing is mandatory before any such recovery can be ordered. Vicarious liability of the State to pay compensation awarded by the MACT is qua the accident victims (claimants) and not qua the employee-driver; the State cannot bypass its own statutory obligations and shift its liability entirely to the driver. The State of Punjab was in violation of its statutory duty under Section 146(3) of the MV Act by exempting its buses from insurance without establishing and maintaining the mandatory compensation fund, and cannot take shelter from this violation to recover from the driver. Issuance of a show cause notice followed by an order without considering the driver's reply does not satisfy the requirement of affording an effective opportunity of being heard; such an order has no legal significance.
Outcome: Both writ petitions allowed. Recovery order dated 24.02.1994 (Annexure P-3) quashed. State impressed upon to either insure its vehicles or establish and maintain a statutory compensation fund under Section 146 MV Act. State told it may recover loss from errant employees only after following proper departmental inquiry procedure with effective opportunity of hearing.
This common judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court (dated 21 December 2013) decides CWP Nos. 12064 of 1994 (Nazar Singh) and 2373 of 1995 (Iqbal Singh), both challenging orders by Punjab Roadways seeking to recover from driver-employees the compensation amounts paid pursuant to MACT awards arising from bus accidents. In the lead case, Nazar Singh drove Punjab Roadways bus PBM-6964 in 1985 when it met with an accident killing two persons; the MACT held him negligent and the employer paid Rs. 3,10,427.95/-. Without holding any departmental inquiry and without meaningfully considering the driver's reply to the show cause notice, Punjab Roadways ordered recovery of the entire amount from the driver in 1994. The court quashed the recovery orders on two grounds. First, the State of Punjab exempted its buses from compulsory insurance under Section 146(3) MV Act without establishing the mandatory statutory compensation fund; having failed its own statutory obligation, the State could not pass its financial liability to the driver. Second, the MACT award was made on a preponderance-of-evidence standard not equivalent to a criminal conviction or departmental inquiry; the employer must hold a proper departmental inquiry with natural justice principles before recovering from an employee. The court directed that recovery from errant drivers is permissible only after following appropriate punishment rules and giving effective hearing, and impressed upon the State the obligation to insure its vehicles or establish the required statutory fund.
