Case: Jagdish Rai vs State of Punjab and Others
Court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh (2009)
Legal area: service_employment; stage: writ
Issues: vicarious_liability, section_166, other
Stance: neutral
Facts: Petitioner Jagdish Rai was a government driver employed with the Assistant Excise and Taxation Commissioner, Muktsar On 4.10.1991, while driving government Jeep No. PAR-782 from Fazilka to Ferozepur, an accident occurred resulting in death of Constable Ranjit Singh FIR registered under Section 304; petitioner was acquitted in criminal trial on 27.2.1999 Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Ferozepur awarded compensation of Rs. 2,49,600/- against petitioner and respondents jointly and severally under Sections 166 and 140 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 State paid the full compensation without filing an appeal; petitioner also did not challenge the award On 26.11.1998, respondent No. 3 directed recovery of Rs. 83,200/- (1/3rd share) from petitioner's salary at Rs. 2,700/- per month without issuing prior notice or conducting any inquiry
Holdings: Recovery from a government employee's salary for pecuniary loss caused by negligence is a minor penalty under Rule 5(iii) of the Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970, requiring prior notice and opportunity of hearing under Rule 10 Acquittal in criminal proceedings does not absolve a driver from civil liability for compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act The State as employer has vicarious liability when its driver causes injury to a third party while driving in the course of employment
Outcome: Writ petition allowed. Order dated 26.11.1998 directing salary recovery quashed. Respondents at liberty to proceed in accordance with law after following mandatory procedure under Punjab Civil Service Rules.
This writ petition under Article 226 was filed by a government driver challenging an order directing recovery of Rs. 83,200 from his salary. The petitioner had been involved in a motor vehicle accident on 4.10.1991 resulting in the death of Constable Ranjit Singh while driving a government Jeep in official duty. Though acquitted in criminal proceedings on 27.2.1999, the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal awarded Rs. 2,49,600 against the petitioner and others jointly and severally. After the State paid the compensation, it sought recovery of the petitioner's one-third share from his salary, issuing a direction without prior notice or inquiry as required by Rule 10 of the Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970. The Court examined the Supreme Court's principles on vicarious liability of government employers in motor accident cases, and held that such salary recovery constitutes a minor penalty under Rule 5(iii) of the Rules, which mandatorily requires notice, opportunity to make representation, and a recorded finding before imposition. Since the mandatory procedure was not followed, the recovery order was quashed and the State was directed to re-proceed in accordance with law.

Case: Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd vs C.C.E., Raipur
Court: Customs Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi (2009)
Legal area: tax_excise; stage: appeal
Issues: excise_duty, other
Stance: mixed
Facts: Monnet Ispat manufactured sponge iron and other iron and steel products chargeable to central excise duty under Chapter 72 and availed Cenvat credit under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 Department issued show cause notice dated 3.11.2006 seeking to deny service tax credit of Rs. 4,36,650 and impose penalty under Rule 15 of Cenvat Credit Rules Assistant Commissioner allowed credit of Rs. 3,98,142 but disallowed Rs. 38,510 for five categories of services including marine inland transit insurance, money insurance, personnel accident insurance, follow-up installation services, and telephone services at GM residence and guest house Commissioner (Appeals) vide order dated 9.10.2007 upheld the Assistant Commissioner's order in full Appellant contended that the disallowed services fall within the definition of 'input service' under the Cenvat Credit Rules and that transit insurance for capital goods is covered when inward transportation is expressly covered
Holdings: When inward transportation of capital goods is specifically covered by the definition of input service, transit insurance during inward transport of those capital goods is also covered Insurance of money in transit from factory to bank is part of the business activity and is covered by the definition of input service Follow-up services for installation of captive power plant are business auxiliary services eligible for Cenvat credit as they relate to setting up or modernisation Accident insurance for contract workers engaged in the factory is eligible where the principal employer has vicarious liability under the Factory Act Telephone services at the GM's residence and guest house are not eligible as no nexus with manufacturing activity was demonstrated
Outcome: Appeal partly allowed. Cenvat credit held eligible for marine inland transit insurance, money insurance in transit, follow-up installation services for captive power plant, and accident insurance for factory personnel including contract workers. Credit denied and penalty upheld for telephone services at GM's residence and company guest house.
This excise appeal before CESTAT was filed by Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. against denial of Cenvat credit under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 for five categories of services. The Assistant Commissioner and Commissioner (Appeals) had disallowed credit of Rs. 38,510 for: marine inland transit insurance for captive power plant machinery transported from BHEL's premises to the appellant's factory; money insurance for cash in transit between factory and bank; follow-up services for installation of the captive power plant; accident insurance for personnel including contract workers; and telephone services at the General Manager's residence and company guest house. The Tribunal held that transit insurance for capital goods is covered by the definition of input service since inward transportation is expressly included. Money-in-transit insurance was held to be a normal prudent business activity covered as input service. Follow-up installation services qualified as business auxiliary services for setting up. Accident insurance for contract workers was held eligible on account of the principal employer's vicarious liability under the Factory Act. However, telephone services at non-factory premises with no demonstrated nexus to manufacturing were rightly denied. The appeal was accordingly allowed in part and the penalty qua the denied credit upheld.

Case: K. Surappa vs V. Venkatesha Reddy and Others
Court: High Court of Karnataka (1995)
Legal area: motor_accident; stage: appeal
Issues: vicarious_liability, rash_negligent_driving, insurance_liability, owner_liability, third_party_liability, compensation_quantum
Vehicles: bus
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Petitioner K. Surappa, a police constable, was travelling in bus No. MYY 3122 belonging to first respondent V. Venkatesha Reddy for election duty on 7.3.1971 Bus was requisitioned by the Deputy Commissioner under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act for transporting election officials and boxes The bus dashed against a roadside tree and capsized due to rash or negligent driving of the driver, causing compound fracture of both bones of petitioner's left leg and a simple fracture Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal dismissed the claim holding: (a) master-servant relationship between owner and driver was temporarily suspended during requisition, and (b) State had sovereign immunity for tortious acts in exercise of sovereign function Insurer also contended that commandeering of vehicle for election purposes was outside the policy cover No evidence was adduced by the owner that he was not required to pay the driver's wages during the requisition period
Holdings: Mere requisitioning of a vehicle by government under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act does not suspend or extinguish the master-servant relationship between the vehicle owner and his driver When a vehicle along with its driver is effectively given on hire for a temporary period, the driver does not cease to be the employee of the owner; the relationship only ends if the hirer also controls the method of driving, not merely the destination The insurer's defence that commandeering for election purposes took the vehicle outside the policy cover was rightly rejected by the Tribunal under Section 96(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act The question of the State's sovereign immunity was rendered unnecessary to decide once owner's vicarious liability was established
Outcome: Appeal allowed with costs. Judgment and award of Tribunal rejecting claim set aside. Petitioner awarded Rs. 20,000 with 12% interest per annum from date of filing petition to date of payment. Insurer (fifth respondent) liable for Rs. 5,000 with proportionate costs and interest; balance payable by owner (first respondent).
This appeal was filed by K. Surappa, a police constable, seeking compensation for injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident on 7.3.1971 when a bus requisitioned by the Deputy Commissioner for election duty capsized due to rash and negligent driving. The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal had dismissed the claim on two grounds: that the requisition temporarily suspended the master-servant relationship between the bus owner and driver, and that the State enjoyed sovereign immunity for tortious acts during a sovereign function. The insurer also pleaded that commandeering placed the vehicle outside the policy cover. The Karnataka High Court reversed all these findings. Applying the principle from Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, the Court held that mere requisitioning under statute does not sever the employer-employee relationship; the burden rests heavily on the owner to prove transfer of the servant and no such evidence was led. The Court further noted that Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act only contemplated requisitioning the vehicle and not the driver's services. The insurer's defence was rejected under Section 96(2). The claimant was awarded Rs. 20,000 with 12% interest, with the insurer bearing Rs. 5,000 per the policy endorsement and the owner the balance.

Case: Ajay Alias Vishal Veeru Devgan vs The Artists Planet & Ors
Court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi (2025)
Legal area: trademark_ip; stage: interlocutory_application
Issues: trademark_infringement, passing_off, personality_rights
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Plaintiff Ajay Devgn is an acclaimed Bollywood actor with a career spanning over four decades, recipient of multiple National Film Awards and the Padma Shri Plaintiff holds registered trademarks for his name 'Ajay Devgn'/'Ajay Devgan'/'Ajay Veeru Devgn' and variations under various classes, and has personality rights over his name, voice, likeness and image Identified infringing defendants include: a website offering fake appearance/performance bookings, sellers of unauthorized merchandise, a YouTube channel creating deepfake content, Facebook pages posting AI-generated images in unsavoury scenarios, and pornographic websites posting face-morphed content Defendant No. 7 (Google LLC/YouTube) impleaded on account of its 'Your content & third-party training' policy allowing creators to use videos for AI-model training, posing risk of propagating defamatory content Defendants are using plaintiff's name, image and persona for commercial gain through unauthorized merchandise sales, deepfakes, AI-generated advertisements and pornographic content without plaintiff's consent The Court noted that some infringing posts dated back to June 2025 and the plaintiff had not availed the IT Intermediary Rules grievance mechanism before approaching the court
Holdings: Celebrity status grants the plaintiff proprietary rights over his personality and associated attributes including name, likeness, voice and image Plaintiff's personality traits are protectable elements of personality rights and he is entitled to injunction against their use for commercial gain without authorisation Plaintiff is prima facie entitled to protect himself against morphed and distorted AI-generated content that portrays him in a repugnant manner Complainants who approach the court without first availing the statutory IT Intermediary Rules mechanism for certain categories of infringing content may be held not entitled to ex-parte ad-interim injunction
Outcome: Ex-parte ad-interim injunction granted against all identified infringing defendants. Directions issued to take down infringing content within 72 hours. Social media intermediaries (YouTube/Google, Meta, X) directed to act if uploaders fail to comply. ISPs directed via MeiTY/DoT to block infringing domains. Court issued prospective observation that plaintiffs bypassing IT Intermediary Rules mechanism for certain categories of posts may be denied ex-parte injunctions in future.
Bollywood actor Ajay Devgn filed this commercial suit (CS(COMM) 1269/2025) seeking permanent injunction and interim relief against 17 defendants infringing his personality, publicity, trademark, and copyright rights. The infringement took multiple forms: unauthorized merchandise bearing his name and image, deepfake videos, AI-generated pornographic content, impersonation on social media, and commercial exploitation of his persona without consent. The plaintiff holds registered trademarks for variations of his name and asserts personality rights under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution, moral rights under Sections 38-38B of the Copyright Act, and statutory trademark rights. The Court granted ex-parte ad-interim injunction against identified infringing defendants, directing takedown of infringing content within 72 hours, and ordered social media intermediaries (YouTube/Google, Meta/Facebook, X) to take action if uploaders failed to comply within the granted time. ISPs were directed via MeiTY and DoT to block infringing domains. The Court also issued a significant prospective observation that plaintiffs who bypass the IT Intermediary Rules grievance mechanism for certain categories of content before approaching the court risk being denied ex-parte ad-interim injunctions in future proceedings.

Case: New Balance Athletics Inc. vs Ashok Kumar & Ors.
Court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi (2024)
Legal area: trademark_ip; stage: suit
Issues: trademark_infringement, passing_off
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: New Balance Athletics Inc. is a US-based footwear company using the trademark 'NEW BALANCE' since 1951 and 'NB' device marks since the 1970s, with registrations in India Defendants Indramani Sahu and Jagabandhu Sahoo operated website www.luxurytag.in which openly sold counterfeit footwear bearing the plaintiff's marks The website explicitly described itself as 'India's first online store to sell replica of all kind (Since 2015)' and admitted selling products 'which look similar to the originals' A representative of the plaintiff placed a test order in February 2023 and confirmed the product received was a fake/counterfeit Main contesting defendants (Nos. 1 and 11) were served but failed to appear or file any written statement despite service on 08.09.2023 and 02.09.2023 respectively Other defendants (proforma defendants) had either complied with court directions or had their right to file written statements closed
Holdings: Where defendants use marks identical to plaintiff's registered trademarks on identical goods sold to identical consumers through identical channels, the triple/quadruple identity test under Section 29(2)(c) read with 29(3) is satisfied and likelihood of confusion is presumed Defendants' explicit self-admissions on their website of selling replica/counterfeit products constitute sufficient proof of infringement and passing off Where contesting defendants fail to file a written statement despite service, the plaintiff's submissions stand admitted under Order VIII Rule 10 of the CPC Counterfeiting is a serious economic offence that erodes brand value and misleads consumers, warranting strict treatment and award of actual costs
Outcome: Suit decreed in favour of plaintiff against defendant nos. 1 and 11. Permanent injunction granted. Actual costs of Rs. 14,51,670/- (including court fees of Rs. 2,01,000 and Local Commissioner's fee of Rs. 1,00,000) awarded jointly and severally payable within 8 weeks.
New Balance Athletics Inc., the American footwear company holding registered trademarks 'NEW BALANCE' and 'NB' in India, filed this commercial suit against operators of a rogue website www.luxurytag.in that openly sold counterfeit footwear bearing the plaintiff's marks. The website explicitly described itself as selling replicas 'which look similar to the originals.' The plaintiff's identities of the infringing defendants were established through discovery from proforma defendants, revealing Indramani Sahu as operator and Jagabandhu Sahoo as the UPI payment beneficiary. Despite service in September 2023, the contesting defendants failed to appear or file written statements, allowing the Court to invoke Order VIII Rule 10 CPC and treat the plaintiff's submissions as admitted. The Court found that the triple/quadruple identity test under Section 29(2)(c) read with 29(3) of the Trade Marks Act was satisfied: identical marks, identical goods (footwear), identical consumer base, and identical channels of distribution. The defendants' own website statements constituted clear admissions of selling counterfeit products. Following the coordinate bench's ruling in Puma SE v. Brijendra Singh that counterfeiting is a serious economic offence, the suit was decreed with a permanent injunction and actual litigation costs of Rs. 14,51,670 awarded jointly and severally against the infringing defendants.

Case: Azuga Inc & Anr vs Azuga Telematics LLC & Ors
Court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi (2025)
Legal area: trademark_ip; stage: interlocutory_application
Issues: trademark_infringement, passing_off
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Plaintiff No. 1 Azuga Inc. is a California-based GPS fleet tracking and management company acquired by Bridgestone Americas Inc. in September 2021; Plaintiff No. 2 is its Indian engineering subsidiary based in Bangalore Plaintiff No. 1 holds registered trademark 'AZUGA' in India (Registration No. 6422638) since at least 2012, as well as registrations in the US, Germany, Mexico and the EU Defendant No. 1 Azuga Telematics LLC, founded in 2022 in Jamshedpur, provides identical GPS fleet tracking and management services using the name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' and a similar logo Defendant No. 3 (Senthil Kumar) is a former employee of Plaintiff No. 2; Defendant No. 2 (Aman Kumar) was listed as domain registrant but voluntarily appeared and denied active involvement with Defendant No. 1 Despite cease and desist notice in January 2023, Defendant No. 1 only altered its logo while continuing to use the full 'AZUGA' mark; defendants also copied plaintiff's website UI assets and product photographs on an 'as-is' basis Pre-litigation mediation before Delhi High Court Legal Services Committee resulted in non-starter report dated 27.05.2025 as defendants failed to appear
Holdings: Adoption of the name 'AZUGA' in identical services as that of the plaintiff's by defendants (including a former employee), prima facie appears mala fide Defendants' use of a deceptively similar mark is likely to mislead the public into believing an association with the plaintiffs, causing confusion and diluting the distinctive character of the AZUGA brand Defendants copying website images on an 'as-is' basis constitutes infringement of plaintiff's copyright in the product photographs Prima facie case established; balance of convenience lies in plaintiff's favour and irreparable harm established
Outcome: Ex-parte ad-interim injunction granted. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 restrained from using the 'AZUGA' mark or any deceptively similar mark including the tradename 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' for GPS fleet tracking services, and from copying plaintiff's copyright-protected website images. Defendant No. 4 (BigRock) directed to lock and suspend Defendant No. 1's domain https://azugatelematicsllc.com/.
California-based Azuga Inc. and its Indian subsidiary Azuga Telematics Private Limited (acquired by Bridgestone in 2021) filed this suit against Azuga Telematics LLC, a Jamshedpur-based GPS fleet management startup founded in 2022, for trademark infringement and copyright infringement. The plaintiff holds registered trademark 'AZUGA' in India since 2012 and reported global revenues of USD 83 million in 2024. The defendants, allegedly connected to former employees of the plaintiff, adopted the near-identical trade name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' for identical GPS fleet tracking services and copied the plaintiff's website UI assets and product photographs on an 'as-is' basis. Despite cease and desist notices and an attempted pre-litigation mediation (which the defendants failed to attend), the infringement continued. Defendant No. 2 appeared voluntarily through video conferencing, denied active involvement with Defendant No. 1, and offered to cooperate. The Court, finding prima facie evidence of mala fide adoption of the mark, likelihood of confusion, and copyright infringement in the copied website images, granted an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 from using the 'AZUGA' mark for GPS fleet tracking services and directed the domain registrar (BigRock) to lock and suspend the defendants' domain.

Case: Intel Corporation vs S.P. Gupta and Others
Court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi (2022)
Legal area: trademark_ip; stage: suit
Issues: trademark_infringement, passing_off, maintainability
Stance: claimant_supporting
Facts: Intel Corporation (USA, incorporated 1968) is the world's leading developer and manufacturer of microprocessors; it has used the mark 'INTEL' since inception and holds trademark registrations in India in Classes 9 and 18 In November 2005 the plaintiff discovered that defendant entities (Intel Gas Gadgets P. Ltd., Intel Gas Guards P. Ltd., and Intel Safety Devices), all promoted by S.P. Gupta, were using 'INTEL' as part of their trading names and domain name www.intelgasgadgets.com for LPG regulators, valves and accessories Despite cease and desist letters in November 2005, December 2005 and March 2006, defendants did not respond, prompting the plaintiff to file suit in May 2006 No interim injunction was granted during the pendency of the suit; evidence was recorded and completed by April 2016 During pendency of the suit, the mark 'INTEL' was declared a well-known trademark by the Trade Marks Registry under Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 S.P. Gupta passed away during proceedings; his legal heirs (sons including Punit Gupta) informed the court through counsel that the three entities had ceased business and would not contest if plaintiff waived damages
Holdings: The mark 'INTEL' has been declared a well-known trademark within the meaning of Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 by the Trade Marks Registry Use of the mark 'INTEL' as a trademark and/or part of trading style by the defendants constitutes infringement as also passing off the defendants' products as those of the plaintiff Where the lis no longer exists between the parties and the defendants are willing to suffer permanent injunction, the suit can be decreed in terms of the prayer clause without proceeding to trial
Outcome: Suit decreed for permanent injunction in terms of prayers (i) and (ii) of the plaint. All other reliefs not pressed. Intel Gas Gadgets (P) Ltd. directed to change its name within three months. Decree sheet to be drawn accordingly.
Intel Corporation (USA) filed this trademark infringement suit in 2006 against three Indian entities controlled by S.P. Gupta—Intel Gas Gadgets P. Ltd., Intel Gas Guards P. Ltd., and Intel Safety Devices—that used 'INTEL' as part of their corporate names, trademarks, and domain name for manufacturing and selling LPG regulators, adaptors, valves, and related accessories. Despite cease and desist notices from November 2005 onwards, the defendants did not respond. No interim injunction was granted during the prolonged proceedings. Evidence was recorded by April 2016. Notably, during the pendency of the suit, the Trade Marks Registry declared 'INTEL' a well-known trademark under Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999. After S.P. Gupta's death, his legal heirs instructed counsel that the three entities had ceased business operations and were willing to suffer permanent injunction provided no damages were pursued. The plaintiff agreed not to press for damages or other reliefs. The Court noted that the lis had effectively ceased and decreed the suit for permanent injunction in terms of the prayer clauses. The registered company among the defendants was additionally directed to change its name within three months through the Registrar of Companies.

Case: M/S. Mandvi Co-Op Bank Ltd. vs Nimesh B. Thakore
Court: Supreme Court of India (2010)
Legal area: banking_finance; stage: criminal_appeal
Issues: dishonour_of_cheque, evidence_appreciation, maintainability, criminal_liability
Stance: neutral
Facts: Mandvi Co-Op Bank Ltd. and other complainants had filed complaints under s.138 NI Act for dishonoured cheques Multiple writ petitions and s.482 CrPC applications were filed before the Gujarat High Court by accused and complainants raising procedural questions about s.145 NI Act High Court framed two questions: (A) scope of accused's right under s.145(2) to call witness for examination, and (B) retrospective applicability of s.145 to pending cases High Court also held that accused could give evidence on affidavit analogously to the complainant under s.145(1) Seven appeals arose before the Supreme Court from the High Court judgment
Holdings: When summoned on the application of the accused under s.145(2), the witness's affidavit already on record constitutes examination-in-chief; the accused is limited to cross-examination of the deponent. Sections 143 to 147 inserted by the 2002 Amendment are procedural, not substantive, and apply retrospectively to cases pending on the date they came into force (February 6, 2003). Section 145(1) confers the right to give evidence on affidavit only on the complainant; the High Court erred in reading into the statute a similar right for the accused; courts cannot add words to a statute.
Outcome: Appeal from SLP (Crl.) No. 3915/2006 (by the bank against giving accused the right to tender affidavit evidence) allowed; High Court direction permitting accused to give evidence on affidavit set aside. Remaining six appeals by accused dismissed. Accused's right under s.145(2) is limited to cross-examination; provisions are procedural and retrospective.
The Supreme Court of India considered seven appeals arising from a Gujarat High Court judgment that addressed the procedure for dishonoured cheque trials under Section 145 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, as amended by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002. The Court resolved three issues. First, whether a person summoned under Section 145(2) at the instance of the accused must depose in examination-in-chief before cross-examination. The Court held that the affidavit already on record constitutes examination-in-chief and the accused is limited to cross-examination only. Second, whether Sections 143 to 147 apply retrospectively to cases pending on February 6, 2003, the date of insertion. The Court affirmed these provisions are procedural and therefore retrospective. Third, whether the accused can give evidence on affidavit like the complainant. The Court reversed the High Court, holding that Section 145(1) expressly confers this right only on the complainant, and courts cannot read in words not present in a statute even if the omission appears inadvertent. The judgment emphasises the legislative scheme of Sections 143 to 147 as a special code for expeditious disposal of cheque dishonour cases, cautioning against procedural interpretations that would convert efficiency measures into tools for delay. The appeal by the bank was allowed; the six appeals by accused persons were dismissed.

Case: Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State (Govt. Of NCT Delhi) & Anr.
Court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi (2019)
Legal area: criminal; stage: other
Issues: criminal_liability, maintainability, evidence_appreciation, other
Stance: neutral
Facts: Four FIRs (Nos.45, 47, 53, 54/2003) were registered against petitioners by Special Cell, Delhi Police for credit card cloning and fraud using skimmed data; charge-sheets filed in December 2003 and October 2004 A fifth case (FIR No.454/2013) arose from creation of fake social media IDs and obscene calls, charge-sheeted under IT Act s.66-A and s.67 All five cases had barely progressed in 10-15 years; charges were not formally framed in all cases Credit card fraud accused negotiated a settlement of Rs.12 lakh with HDFC Bank through court-annexed mediation (Patiala House Courts) in 2018; IT Act case settled for Rs.2 lakh through Delhi HC Mediation Centre Petitioners filed five Crl.MC petitions under s.482 CrPC seeking quashing of the FIRs and proceedings based on these settlements
Holdings: Economic offences affecting the financial and economic well-being of the State and its banking institutions cannot be quashed on private settlement under s.482 CrPC, regardless of the complainant's willingness. Offences involving mental depravity (such as obscene calls and IT Act violations) fall outside the category of cases quashable on settlement, especially where the court had previously declined to quash the same proceedings. Before referring a criminal case to mediation, the court must first assess whether a settlement reached through such process could lawfully be acted upon to terminate the criminal proceedings. Mediators must undertake a preliminary scrutiny of the criminal case to determine whether the settlement being facilitated is permissible in law before brokering any agreement.
Outcome: All five petitions under s.482 CrPC dismissed. Quashing of criminal proceedings in credit card fraud cases and IT Act obscene calls case refused. Comprehensive guidelines issued directing courts to assess quashability before referring criminal cases to mediation, and requiring mediators to undertake preliminary scrutiny of permissibility. Four fraud cases directed to be heard on day-to-day basis.
The Delhi High Court consolidated five petitions under Section 482 CrPC seeking quashing of criminal cases on the basis of mediation settlements. Four petitions (Crl.MC 5765, 5768, 5785, 5805/2018) related to FIRs registered in 2003 against accused persons for credit card cloning and fraud using skimmed data, cases that had barely progressed in fifteen years. The fifth petition (Crl.MC 5995/2018) concerned FIR 454/2013 for creation of fake social media IDs and obscene calls under the IT Act. In each case, the accused had reached settlements through court-annexed mediation centres and sought quashing thereafter. The Court declined to quash any of the five proceedings. Reviewing the jurisprudence from Gian Singh, Narinder Singh, Parbatbhai Aahir and related cases, the Court held that economic offences involving credit card fraud affect the financial well-being of the State and public trust in banking; they are not private in nature and cannot be quashed on settlement. The obscene calls offence equally involves mental depravity and falls outside quashable categories. The Court issued comprehensive guidelines directing that before referring criminal cases to mediation, courts must assess whether the offences involved are quashable in law; mediators must conduct preliminary scrutiny before facilitating settlement; and vetting must occur before formal execution of any settlement. The four fraud cases were directed to proceed on day-to-day basis under monitoring of the Sessions Judge.

text:
Case: Company Of Management For Baranagar Jute Factory vs Atis Dipankar Chowdhuri
Court: High Court at Calcutta (1993)
Legal area: banking_finance; stage: revision
Issues: dishonour_of_cheque, maintainability, criminal_liability, limitation
Stance: neutral
Facts: Baranagar Jute Factory was a borrower of the State Bank of India; a winding-up proceeding was initiated and the High Court formed a Committee of Management under a court-approved scheme to run the factory and repay debts by instalments The Committee issued cheque No.776924 dated 29-8-90 on Union Bank of India (Ezra Street) in favour of SBI; the cheque was returned on 11-9-90 with remark 'exceeds arrangement' and again on 23-11-90 with remark 'refer to drawer' SBI wrote to Union Bank confirming insufficient balance, issued a demand notice dated 4-12-90, and the Committee's reply dated 11-12-90 acknowledged receipt but denied liability and raised objections without paying SBI filed a complaint before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Calcutta under s.138 read with s.141 NI Act; cognizance was taken and proceedings began as criminal case No. C/46/1991 Petitioners filed a criminal revision challenging the prosecution on three grounds: timeliness of notice after second presentation, need for court's leave before prosecuting a court-created committee, and whether the Committee qualifies as a 'company' under s.141
Holdings: A second presentation of a dishonoured cheque within the validity period is not prohibited by s.138 NI Act; the payee retains the right to give demand notice and initiate prosecution after the second dishonour. A Committee of Management appointed by the High Court under a court-approved scheme is akin to a court-appointed receiver and cannot be prosecuted without prior leave of the court; prosecution without such leave is bad. A Committee of Management constituted by court order is not a 'company' or body corporate or association of individuals within the meaning of the explanation to s.141 NI Act; no vicarious liability can be fastened on such a committee under that section.
Outcome: Criminal revision allowed. The prosecution against the Committee of Management and its signatory quashed. Proceedings in criminal case No. C/46/1991 under s.138/141 NI Act before the CMC Calcutta set aside; accused petitioners discharged from bail bonds. The court held prosecution was bad for want of prior leave of court and that the Committee of Management is not a 'company' under s.141.
The Calcutta High Court allowed a criminal revision challenging prosecution under Sections 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The petitioners were a Committee of Management of Baranagar Jute Factory, formed by High Court order under a court-approved scheme to manage the insolvent company, and its authorised signatory. The Committee had issued a cheque favouring the State Bank of India (creditor), which was dishonoured twice. SBI served a demand notice after the second dishonour and filed a complaint. The petitioners raised three objections. On the first objection, the Court rejected the argument that the bank's choice to re-present the cheque without sending notice after the first dishonour extinguished the right to prosecute; it held that re-presentation within the validity period is permissible and notice after the second dishonour is valid. On the second objection, the Court held that the Committee of Management, being a creation of the Court equivalent to a receiver, required prior leave of the court before it could be prosecuted; prosecuting without such leave rendered the action bad. On the third objection, the Court held that the Committee of Management is not a 'company', body corporate, firm, or association of individuals as defined in the explanation to Section 141 NI Act, and cannot suffer imprisonment, making vicarious prosecution under that section unavailable. The criminal revision was allowed and the prosecution quashed.

text:
Case: Ashokbhai Shankar Chaudhary & 1 vs Jayendra Virendra Sharma & 1
Court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad (2014)
Legal area: specific_performance; stage: appeal
Issues: specific_performance_relief, maintainability, other
Stance: neutral
Facts: Suit property (Revenue Survey No.544/3, 19260 sq.ft.) was owned in ½ undivided share each by the plaintiff and defendant No.1, who were cousins On 07.03.2007, defendant No.1 entered into a sale agreement to sell his ½ share to the plaintiff for Rs.15 lakhs; plaintiff paid part consideration of Rs.1,50,000 by cheque and claimed to have been put in possession of the entire property Defendant No.1, despite a public notice by him cancelling the sale agreement dated 16.02.2010 (citing plaintiff's failure to pay balance by 29.12.2009), sold his ½ share to defendants 2 and 3 by Registered Sale Deed dated 28.10.2010 for Rs.32 lakhs Defendants 2 and 3 had published a public notice for title clearance on 02.03.2010 before execution of their sale deed Plaintiff filed Special Civil Suit No.263 of 2010 for specific performance and filed two injunction applications (Exh.5 and Exh.37); the trial court granted both applications directing status quo on title and possession
Holdings: Defendants 2 and 3 cannot be characterised as bona fide purchasers under Section 19-B of the Specific Relief Act at this stage as they had notice of the prior sale agreement from a public notice before executing their sale deed. In contracts relating to immovable property, time is ordinarily not the essence of contract and failure to pay balance consideration before a specified date does not render the contract terminable. An appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's discretionary order on injunction unless the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or perversely, or the court ignored settled principles.
Outcome: Both Appeal from Orders (AFO No.196 and 197 of 2014) dismissed. Interim injunction directing status quo on title and possession upheld. Civil applications also dismissed. Defendants 2 and 3 cannot claim bona fide purchaser protection at this stage; time was not the essence of the contract.
The Gujarat High Court dismissed appeals filed by defendants 2 and 3 against an interim injunction order granted in a specific performance suit (Special Civil Suit No.263 of 2010). The plaintiff and defendant No.1 were co-sharers of the suit property. Defendant No.1 had agreed to sell his ½ share to the plaintiff under a sale agreement dated 07.03.2007, receiving part payment. Before the injunction application was heard, defendant No.1 sold his ½ share to defendants 2 and 3 by registered sale deed dated 28.10.2010 for Rs.32 lakhs. The trial court granted status quo on title and possession. Defendants 2 and 3 challenged the injunction claiming bona fide purchaser protection under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act, and arguing that the plaintiff's failure to pay the balance consideration by 29.12.2009 had extinguished the sale agreement. The High Court held that defendants 2 and 3 could not claim bona fide purchaser status as they had notice of the prior sale agreement through a public notice before executing their purchase deed. It also held that in immovable property contracts, time is ordinarily not the essence of the contract and failure to pay by a specified date does not automatically terminate the agreement. Applying the limited scope of Order 43 Rule 1(r) CPC, the appellate court declined to substitute its discretion for that of the trial court in the absence of arbitrariness or perversity. Both appeals were dismissed.

Case: Chinnasamy vs K. Viswanathan (died) and Others
Court: High Court of Judicature at Madras (2020)
Legal area: specific_performance; stage: second_appeal
Issues: specific_performance_relief, evidence_appreciation
Stance: neutral
Facts: Plaintiff claimed to have entered into a sale agreement (Ext.A.1) dated 01.05.1992 to purchase agricultural property belonging to defendants 1 to 3 for Rs.75,000 total, paying Rs.50,000 and receiving possession in continuation of his prior tenancy; balance of Rs.25,000 payable within 11 months Defendants 1 to 3 denied Ext.A.1 and alleged it was fabricated; on 24.09.1992, the second defendant sold the suit property to the fourth defendant by sale deed (Ext.B.1) Defendants 1 to 3 failed to enter the witness box; trial court compared signatures under s.73 Evidence Act, found Ext.A.1 genuine, and decreed specific performance First Appellate Court also found Ext.A.1 genuine but dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiff had not proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract under s.16(C) Specific Relief Act Plaintiff filed second appeal before Madras HC on five substantial questions of law, including burden of proof of bona fide purchase and readiness/willingness
Holdings: A decree for specific performance is a discretionary relief and the plaintiff must satisfy the conscience of the court that he deserves it; the genuineness of the agreement alone does not entitle the plaintiff to a decree. Section 16(C) of the Specific Relief Act casts a statutory burden on the plaintiff to plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract throughout the relevant period; failure to discharge this burden is fatal to the suit. Even if the subsequent purchaser fails to plead the bona fide purchaser defence under s.19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff who seeks equitable relief of specific performance must still prove that the subsequent purchaser had notice of the original agreement.
Outcome: Second appeal dismissed. Judgment and decree of the first Appellate Court (III Additional District Judge, Krishnagiri) dated 12.07.2000 in A.S.No.34 of 1999 reversing the trial court decree upheld. Plaintiff's failure to prove readiness and willingness to perform the contract under s.16(C) Specific Relief Act was determinative; suit for specific performance dismissed.
The Madras High Court dismissed a second appeal in a specific performance suit. The plaintiff, a tenant of agricultural property, claimed to have entered into a sale agreement (Ext.A.1) dated 01.05.1992 paying Rs.50,000 out of Rs.75,000 total consideration and receiving possession. Defendants 1 to 3 (vendors) denied the agreement and sold the property to the fourth defendant by registered sale deed (Ext.B.1) on 24.09.1992. The trial court, finding defendants 1 to 3 failed to contest their signatures in Ext.A.1, decreed specific performance. The first Appellate Court concurrently found Ext.A.1 genuine but dismissed the suit, holding the plaintiff had not proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract. The Madras High Court upheld this finding. Applying Section 16(C) of the Specific Relief Act as it stood at the time of suit, the Court affirmed that a decree for specific performance is a discretionary equitable relief requiring the plaintiff to plead and prove readiness and willingness throughout. The Court further held that even if the fourth defendant failed to plead the bona fide purchaser defence under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff still bore the burden of demonstrating the fourth defendant had notice of Ext.A.1, as he seeks equitable relief and must walk the extra distance to satisfy the court's conscience. Finding no perversity in the first Appellate Court's findings, all five substantial questions of law failed and the second appeal was dismissed.

Case: Smt. Iravva K Purantar vs S. Venkatesh and Kendra Upadyayara Sangha (Regd.)
Court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru (2023)
Legal area: specific_performance; stage: appeal
Issues: specific_performance_relief, maintainability, limitation, other
Stance: neutral
Facts: Respondent No.1/plaintiff instituted O.S.No.3810/2010 against respondent No.2/defendant-Sangha for specific performance of an unregistered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 10.10.1986 in respect of a site property The Sangha's written statement alleged it had separately allotted and alienated the very same site to the appellant (Smt. Iravva K Purantar) under a registered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 17.09.1987 and had issued a possession certificate dated 17.03.1988 The defendant-Sangha neither cross-examined the plaintiff's witness (PW.1) nor led any oral or documentary evidence in support of its defence Trial court, on the basis of uncontroverted evidence of PW.1, decreed the suit for specific performance in favour of the plaintiff by judgment and decree dated 15.12.2015 Appellant (not arrayed as a party to the suit despite the Sangha's own written statement disclosing her claim) filed a Regular First Appeal with a delay of 677 days, along with applications for condonation of delay, permission to appeal, impleadment as additional defendant, and production of additional documents (registered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 17.09.1987, possession certificate, sale deed dated 19.03.2012, katha documents)
Holdings: A non-party to a specific performance suit may be a proper and necessary party, and is entitled to prefer an appeal, where the suit property is the very property in which she claims rights under a competing registered agreement, and the defendant's written statement acknowledges the alienation in her favour but the defendant defaulted in contesting the suit. Delay in filing an appeal by a non-party who had no knowledge of the pendency of the suit and whose competing agreement was registered (unlike the plaintiff's unregistered agreement) constitutes bonafide reason and unavoidable circumstance warranting condonation. Where a non-party with competing rights is impleaded and additional evidence is necessary for adjudication, the proper course under Order 41 Rule 28 CPC is to set aside the impugned decree and remit the matter to the trial court for fresh consideration.
Outcome: Regular First Appeal allowed. Impugned judgment and decree dated 15.12.2015 in O.S.No.3810/2010 set aside. Matter remitted to trial court for reconsideration afresh. Appellant impleaded as additional defendant No.2; additional documents received on record; delay of 677 days condoned; liberty granted to all parties to lead evidence and cross-examine witnesses.
The Karnataka High Court allowed a Regular First Appeal filed by a non-party to a specific performance suit. Respondent No.1/plaintiff had instituted O.S.No.3810/2010 against respondent No.2/defendant (Kendra Upadyayara Sangha, Regd.) for specific performance of an unregistered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 10.10.1986 relating to a site property. The Sangha's written statement admitted it had allotted and alienated the same property to the appellant under a registered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 17.09.1987, but the Sangha neither cross-examined the plaintiff's witness nor led any evidence. The trial court decreed specific performance in the plaintiff's favour. The appellant, who had not been made a party to the suit despite the Sangha's own admission, filed an appeal with a delay of 677 days, seeking impleadment, additional documents on record (including her registered lease-cum-sale agreement, possession certificate and sale deed), and condonation of delay. The High Court held that the delay was due to bonafide reasons since the appellant had no knowledge of the suit and her agreement was a registered document. It found the appellant to be both a proper and necessary party, allowed all interlocutory applications, and set aside the impugned decree. The matter was remitted to the trial court for fresh consideration with the appellant impleaded as additional defendant No.2, with liberty to all parties to adduce evidence.

Case: Kum. H. Supriya vs S. Krishnappa and Others
Court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru (2026)
Legal area: civil_procedure; stage: writ
Issues: amendment_of_pleadings, specific_performance_relief
Stance: neutral
Facts: O.S.No.7/2018 was instituted by respondent No.1/plaintiff before the Senior Civil Judge and JMFC, Holenarasipura, for specific performance of a sale agreement dated 14.09.2018 relating to immovable property, against defendant Nos.1, 2 and 3 The plaintiff had adduced evidence and cross-examination of PW1 (plaintiff's witness) was at an advanced stage when the petitioner/defendant No.3 filed I.A.No.VIII under Order 6 Rule 17 read with s.151 CPC seeking amendment of the written statement The proposed amendment incorporated additional paragraph No.17a after paragraph 17, relating to certain subsequent events including the pendency of O.S.No.59/2021 before the Senior Civil Judge, Holenarasipura The plaintiff opposed the amendment application; the trial court rejected I.A.No.VIII by impugned order dated 17.11.2025 on the ground that the petitioner had not exercised due diligence in not seeking the amendment earlier Petitioner/defendant No.3 challenged the rejection order by Writ Petition No.37035 of 2025 under Article 227 of the Constitution
Holdings: An application to amend a written statement to incorporate subsequent events that arose after the institution of the suit cannot be refused on the ground of lack of due diligence, since such events obviously could not have been pleaded at the time of filing the original written statement. Refusal of an amendment relating to subsequent events occasions failure of justice warranting interference under Article 227 of the Constitution, particularly when the plaintiff suffers no prejudice as she can file a rejoinder to the amended written statement.
Outcome: Writ petition allowed. Impugned order dated 17.11.2025 rejecting I.A.No.VIII in O.S.No.7/2018 set aside. I.A.No.VIII under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC allowed. Liberty granted to respondent No.1/plaintiff to file rejoinder/reply to the amended written statement. Trial court directed to dispose of the suit within one year from receipt of copy of this order.
The Karnataka High Court allowed a writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution filed by defendant No.3 in a specific performance suit (O.S.No.7/2018) pending before the Senior Civil Judge and JMFC, Holenarasipura. The underlying suit was filed by the plaintiff for specific performance of a sale agreement dated 14.09.2018 relating to immovable property. After the plaintiff had led evidence and cross-examination of PW1 was underway, the petitioner/defendant No.3 filed I.A.No.VIII under Order 6 Rule 17 read with Section 151 CPC to amend the written statement by adding a paragraph incorporating certain subsequent events including the pendency of another suit, O.S.No.59/2021, arising after institution of the present suit. The trial court rejected the amendment on the ground that the petitioner had not exercised due diligence by not seeking the amendment earlier. The High Court set aside this order, holding that an amendment to incorporate events that arose after institution of the suit could not be refused on the ground of lack of due diligence since those events could not have been pleaded in the original written statement filed in 2018. Following the principles in LIC v. Sanjeev Builders, Dinesh Goyal v. Suman Agarwal, and a co-ordinate bench ruling, the Court found that refusal of the amendment occasioned failure of justice. No prejudice to the plaintiff was found as the plaintiff could file a rejoinder. I.A.No.VIII was allowed and the trial court was directed to dispose of the suit within one year.
